maintopic: MR. GREGOIRE-ENGLISH SPEAKING CONDUCTORS ON OTTAWA-MONTREAL TRAIN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: MR. GREGOIRE-ENGLISH SPEAKING CONDUCTORS ON OTTAWA-MONTREAL TRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege on my own behalf and also on behalf of all French Canadian members of this house.
Yesterday afternoon I received a visit from a few students from the University of Montreal and, while they were in my office I did my best to convince them that bilingualism was making headway within the federal government and the crown corporations. In fact I almost had them convinced that considerable progress had been achieved in that field.
However, a few minutes later with the same students I boarded the 5.20 p.m. C.N. train which runs between Ottawa and Montreal, two cities with a very large proportion of French speaking people. However, I was most disappointed and humiliated when I noticed that the two conductors on that train did not speak a single word of French. Needless to say, I was subjected to the sarcasm of those students whom I had tried to convince that bilingualism was growing within crown corporations. They were especially critical about the Quebec members of parliament who, they said, were making no headway in their representations to the federal government. Such representations, they said, were merely a subject of derision.
I therefore ask the Prime Minister to have an inquiry made in that respect so that steps may be taken to prevent the recurrence of such a situation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration regarding a story which appears in this morning's issue of a Toronto newspaper concerning a Jamaican nurse's aid who came to Canada from England about a year ago and who has been denied permission to bring her two children. The ground given by the special immigration inquiry officer was that these children were illegitimate. He is quoted as having said that Jamaicans were not allowed to enter Canada if they had children who were born out of wedlock. I want to ask the minister if the decision in this case, which was heard last Friday by the immigration appeal board, has been upheld and, if so, would the minister not agree with the statement made in this newspaper report that this whole business smacks of injustice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: DENIAL OF PERMISSION TO BRING IN CHILDREN OF JAMAICAN IMMIGRANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as soon as my attention was drawn to the events which took place in Toronto with regard to Miss Daisy Maud Henry, I asked my officials to supply full particulars on the case.
First of all, I would like to say that all the proceedings instituted in Toronto, either at the time of the inquiry or at the time of the appeal, were based solely on the fact that when Miss Henry filed her application for admission to Canada she failed to mention that she had two children. All subsequent proceedings were of a technical nature and dealt with the fact that Miss Henry is alleged to have made a false statement, which effect was to disqualify her for admission to Canada.
Now at no time was action taken by the investigating officers, or by the court of appeal, which might lead to believe that Miss Henry was being discriminated against in any way.
On the other hand, the newspaper Globe and Mail reported certain statements made by some high official of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I admit that if these words were spoken about a person who is not of the white race, the matter is very serious and, as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration I shall see to it that the official concerned, if in fact he did say these words,
Inquiries of the Ministry bears the consequences of such an attitude toward a person who is not of the white race.
Let me say then that the case was judged by a court of appeal and that it has now reached my office. In my capacity of minister I shall be able to use my discretion in reaching a final decision in the case of Miss Henry..

speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: BANFF-MEETING WITH COUNCIL RESPECTING MOTEL CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the adjournment last week I have had an opportunity to read the speech of my colleague from Burn-aby-Richmond in which he dealt in general with the policies of the government. I do not want to repeat any of those matters, except to say that I certainly endorse the views that he expressed.
This afternoon I would like to lay before the committee a problem that concerns almost every household in Canada, and urge upon the government that some action be taken to meet the problem. I am referring, of course, to the old problem of the consumer in Canada and the extent to which he is deprived of adequate protection against such things as unfair packaging, high interest rates and a general lack of information upon which he can make an intelligent choice. The size of this group is to me astonishing. The recent studies that are available indicate that approximately 90 per cent of the personal disposable income of Canadians is used to directly satisfy the demands of individual consumers for goods and services. This represents two thirds of our gross national product and amounts to some $27 billion each year being spent by the consumers in Canada.
It is therefore obvious that this group is represented in every household in Canada, and it is urgently necessary that something be done to deal with the problems they face. At the present time the government is active in the general consumer field, but the degree of activity is so scattered among the various

departments that it is very doubtful that any really cohesive plan can be developed for the consumer market. For example, the Department of Trade and Commerce has a weights and measures division; the Department of Agriculture has a consumer section and a section for the inspection of meat and other foods; the Department of Justice has an anti-combines section for price fixing, which is relatively ineffective; the Department of National Health and Welfare has its food and drug directorate; the Department of Defence Production has a consumer section; the Department of Fisheries has an information and consumer branch. In short, Mr. Chairman, while there is activity in this field, it is scattered among all the government departments.
The suggestion I would like to put to the government is that they create a department of consumer affairs, headed by a full time minister to devote all his attention to the affairs of this new and important department. As you know, Mr. Chairman, every other economic group in Canada has a department to speak for it. We have the Department of Trade and Commerce, concerned with business in general; we have the Department of Industry; we have the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Labour. All these departments deal with important organized groups in the community, but for the consumer there is nobody to speak on his behalf, at least in any co-ordinated way. We feel very strongly that the time has come for the creation of a new department of consumer affairs.
This, of course, is not our own idea alone; members of the house in speeches outside the house have advocated a similar program. The hon. member for Northumberland in a recent speech advocated such a change; the consumers association of Canada has advocated such a change; the credit union associations of Canada have made representations to the government along the same line. All these groups have tried to point out to the government the urgent problems of this important section of the community and the very real need for a special department to handle their affairs.
It is interesting that the United States is again ahead of us in this whole field. In that country there has been an enormous amount of research undertaken, and various legislative acts have been passed for the protection of the consumer. We should like to suggest to the government that they bring into effect
Supply-Trade and Commerce a bill of rights for the consumer setting out what are his rights in the jungle of the competitive trade world.
I think there are four basic rights. First of all, the consumer ought to have the right to safety, to be protected against the marketing of goods which are hazardous to health or life. Second, the consumer should have the right to be informed; to be protected against fraudulent, deceitful or grossly misleading information, advertising, labelling or other practices; and above all to be given the facts he needs to make an informed choice. Third, the consumer ought to have the right to choose; the right to be assured wherever possible access to a variety of products and services at competitive prices; and in those industries in which competition is not workable-and there are many-a government regulation substituted constituting an assurance of satisfactory quality and service at fair prices. Finally, the consumer must have the right to be heard; to be assured that the consumer's interest will receive full and sympathetic consideration in the formulation of government policy and fair and expeditious treatment in its administrative tribunals. I think if we were to bring into effect a bill of rights for the consumer we would go a long way toward dealing with this very important problem.
There have been various voluntary agencies at work in Canada, the most notable being, of course, the Canadian consumers association. This organization has done a great deal of work in testing various products which are on the market and in making the information available to the general public. But it is handicapped for money and just does not have the tremendous machinery for publication that is available to the government.
I am thinking of some of the tests they have made. For example, they recently issued a statement declaring that they had conducted tests of thermometers of Japanese or German origin. These thermometers bore the following statement: "This clinical thermometer has been rigidly inspected and tested in accordance with standards established by the national research council". On examination, Mr. Chairman, it turned out that none of the thermometers which bore this guarantee passed all the C.A.C. tests, and the C.A.C. magazine concluded that they considered this to be misleading to consumers and that it was contrary to the section of the Canadian Criminal Code which forbids the use of the national research council's

Supply-Trade and Commerce name in advertising unless all its specifications are met. This is just one of dozens of examples where the public are being hoodwinked by this type of fraudulent advertising.
In other cases the same organization, the consumers association of Canada, conducted tests, for example on cans of fruit juice, and it was found that of the 20 ounce cans in particular which were tested only one in every nine contained the full 20 ounces. Again there was a whole series of misleading representations on the packaging. Although one particular instance does not sound very serious, when this is multiplied millions of times over, thus reflecting the quantity of sales, it is evident that the public are being gypped and fraudulently treated.
The same organization conducted tests on milk cartons and found that the contents of the cartons which were investigated varied in amount all the way down to four fluid ounces below the amount specified on the label. Thirteen brands were found to be below the amount advertised, which again is another flagrant example of how consumers are gypped. The files of those interested in this subject are bulging with examples of fraudulent and misleading advertising to which the public are being subjected by various companies, apparently with immunity to our present laws.
Another tricky gimmick which is used is to state the number of ounces contained in the various packages. Indeed, to analyse them the housewife would need to have an I.B.M. computer in order to establish whether the various ranges were competitive. These are some examples which can be seen at any of our local general stores. Spic and Span have a one pound three and a half ounce package for 41 cents, a two pound eight ounce package for 82 cents and a four pound six and a half ounce package for $1.40. How on earth is the housewife in the busy rush of the day going to divide up all the fractions of ounces so as to decide whether one package is more economic than another? Surf sells a two pound 10 ounce package for 73 cents and a five pound package for $1.19. Again, how is the shopper to divide the fractions back and forth? Another example; Colgate toothpaste sells at 44 grams for 39 cents, 82 grams for 61 cents, 162 grams for 94 cents and 238 grams for $1.19. Again how is the housewife to break this down so as to establish whether or not there is a proper price relationship for the product? Pepsodent toothpaste sells at 41 grams for 33 cents and 80.5 grams for 59


cents. How is there any assurance of a properly calculated price unless the housewife takes a calculating machine to the cashier's desk with her? Another example; Clover Leaf pink salmon, three and three quarter ounces for 25 cents, seven and three quarter ounces for 35 cents and 15J ounces for 69 cents. I challenge anyone but a brilliant mathematician to do the fast calculations required to establish whether this is a proper competitive price.
I have a whole list of these examples here, Mr. Chairman, which I could read into the record, but I do not intend to do so because I think it is quite clear that this business of the broken ounces and the variations in price make it absolutely impossible for the consumers of Canada to know whether they are being gypped or are in fact getting true measure. We are all aware of the gimmick on the package which declares "10 cents off" or "15 cents off," whatever it may be. We can all go into a supermarket and buy a large can of coffee which has on the label "10 cents off," or "15 cents off." In fact these printed labels are part of the package itself and bear no relationship whatever to the price paid by the consumer. In short it is another gimmick to hoodwink the public.
Those of us who are serving on the special committee on consumer credit along with the gentlemen of the other place are already shocked and dismayed at the evidence which has been given of the degree to which Canadian consumers are not aware of the interest charges which they are paying. All of us are astounded at the mountainous rate of interest being gouged out of the Canadian public through lack of disclosure, hidden bonuses, special charges, all of which are lumped together in the price of the product being sold. So as I say I think the housewives and the general consumers of Canada simply do not have the faintest idea whether or not they are being properly protected. Indeed, the whole business of the way in which goods are packaged and the housewife defrauded is, in my view, something which comes down to the responsibility of this government.
As I have said, the late President Kennedy was very aware of this problem, and early in his term of office sent a message to the United States congress in which he accepted on behalf of the federal government that the federal government, by its very nature, was the highest spokesman for all the people; and he accepted the principle that the federal government has a responsibility to the unspoken-for consumer to see that ade-

quate legislation is brought in and that adequate provision is made for his protection.
Clearly, Mr. Chairman, if there is going to be any serious attempt on our part to get into this subject it simply cannot be done by leaving the problems of the consumer in the hands of each individual minister in so far as they relate to their departments. All we will have by doing so is a disjointed and generally chaotic approach to a $27 billion industry. It seems to me that the representations which have been made by various groups to the government ought to receive serious consideration.
We should like to suggest, for example, that the post office be used for the displaying of information which would be useful to the consumer. There is already a great deal of material that could be made available to the consumer. Second, we should like to see stiffer laws, for example, for the testing of drugs and cosmetics before they reach the public. All of us will remember the thalidomide tragedy of a year or so ago. All of us will want to see that never again will there be any possibility of anything of this sort getting on the market. We should like to see a re-examination of this kind of thing before it is allowed on the market, because there is nothing so cruel as to permit the sale of useless material, or material which will perhaps do harm.
We should also like to see stiffer laws in respect of credit abuses. Many members in all sections of this house have introduced bills calling for greater disclosure of interest charges so the buyer will know precisely what he is paying for the money he is borrowing. I have yet to see any formula which would work, other than the one proposed by the credit union league representatives when they appeared before the special committee on consumer credit. They did produce a formula which would make this clear. We should like to see some limitation upon interest charges generally. We realize this is a dangerous area, because in many ways we merely drive the money supply somewhere else, but something should be done about an upper limit on gross interest charges.
We should like to see some consideration given on behalf of the consumer to the opening up of alternative credit sources. I understand, for example, that chartered banks would be very interested in getting into the field of consumer credit, and would provide it at less than one half the price Canadians are now paying, if certain changes in the Bank Act could be brought in. We hope to 20220-562
Supply-Trade and Commerce raise this question when the Bank Act is under revision.
We should like to see something done in the form of the truth in packaging legislation which has been introduced in the United States. There has been considerable discussion there in this regard, and I think it was Senator Hart who pioneered in this field. He has introduced an excellent bill called the truth in packaging bill, which goes through all the abuses to which the consumers are now subjected and attempts to regulate the exploitation that is taking place. I think there is a good lesson to be learned here so far as our internal commercial policies are concerned.
We should like to see a department of this kind have an up to date statistical flow of information concerning the whole field of consumer credit. Many of the economic shifts that have taken place in Canada have been due to the very pronounced change in the pattern of spending of Canadian consumers. After all, when there is a shift in the method of spending by a group who consume $27 billion worth of goods and services, there is a profound effect upon the economy of the country as a whole.
I do not want to labour this point because I think an examination of the record and the information already available will make it very clear that there is an urgent need for something to be done in this field. I hope if the minister does not feel this is strictly within the terms of reference of his department he will at least pass it on to whoever in government should give it consideration.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I merely want to summarize the proposals we have suggested. 1. That a new department of consumer affairs be created with a full time minister to look after the affairs of the consumers of Canada as a whole, because at the present time there is nobody to speak for them.
2.	A bill of rights should be adopted for the consumers to set out and guarantee to them those things I raised earlier in my speech.
3.	We suggest the introduction of the necessary legislation to deal with credit, unfair packaging, distasteful advertising, and all the other abuses to which the consuming public is being subjected at the present time.
4.	We suggest such a department should be operated in co-operation with provincial agencies which now exist in order to be sure that the ultimate amount of consumer protection will be made available.
5.	We want to urge that a really serious examination be made of this problem by the
8876	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce government rather than just the active consideration to which reference has been made on orders of the day. We urge that a serious attempt be made to give representation to this tremendous section of Canada, which at the present time is unrepresented, but whose problems affect the lives of every Canadian.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been inspired to make a few comments during our consideration of the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce because of certain things that have taken place recently, one being the statement made by the minister.
First of all I should like to thank the minister and congratulate him for his statement to this house last week, in which he included a list of the achievements of the Conservative administration which preceded his. He was very courteous in pointing out in his opening sentence that Canada is now in the fourth year of advance and is moving strongly ahead. Thank heaven most of us can subtract and look back to the spring of 1961, when this advance received tremendous impetus by the budget of that year.
Even though all the things the Conservative administration did are not listed in those opening remarks, when one goes through his speech and picks off all the items he did mention, including the so-called power policy, national oil policy, the balancing of the merchandise account trade balance, and general economic improvement, I think the minister should be congratulated for bringing these to public attention, and for noting that the efforts made by the previous government to carry out a policy of expansion to meet our world commitments on balance of payments was the right course to follow.
I do not intend in my remarks to discuss the obvious schizophrenia of the present government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce talks in one language while the Minister of Finance talks in another language, which is restrictive. If one looks at the statements of the Minister of Finance which are included in the royal commission report- particularly the preliminary report, and repeated in a more general fashion in the final report-the minister's statements made in his paper read to the Kingston conference of 1960, and the statements made in the minister's book "Troubled Canada"-which I call Mein Kampf; then if one looks at the recent actions of the Minister of Finance, he will see a government under the control of policies leading toward restriction. This is the wrong policy for Canada.


The Minister of Trade and Commerce speaks in an entirely different language. He speaks of multilateral trade. That is a sound policy and the only course that Canada should follow if we are to consider our national interests.
I think on this occasion I should put forward those proposals which I believe are of interest to the Department of Trade and Commerce and to the whole country. In my opinion the world is at the crossroads of decision so far as trade is concerned. Ever since the time of the industrial revolution trade has developed tremendously among those nations which can be classified as industrial. They have learned the hard way that they have to work together, and in working together there have been tremendous achievements.
But a new factor has now entered the picture. This new factor is that there are a tremendous number of new countries which are not industrialized to any great extent and whose people cry out for a better standard of living. This is the quandary in which Canada finds itself. We have such tremendous volumes of energy and resources, and we know that all the fingers of the world are pointing at us and wondering which course we will take.
There are two main paths that the nations seem to be considering. One is the traditional path whereby industrial nations gather together in various groupings, primarily GATT. They look at the world from their vantage point of rich living and progress. They are aware of the new nations on the outside, and they condescend to look at the problems of the newly developing nations and wonder how they can let some of their products into this rich men's club without seriously lowering the standard of living within the magic circle. This is the one path. Each one of the people sent by Canada to the hard and heavy negotiations in Geneva concerning new agreements under GATT is sent there with instructions that he must get the best possible deal for his country and make it as difficult as possible for anybody else to get into our markets.

To sell at any cost is the philosophy with which they are sent there. This is the direction that ministers, not only under the present government, give them. It is a traditional policy of all the western industrial nations.
I suggest that the other path should be looked at. This other path is a strange, new

one. It is based on an attitude of mind just the reverse of what I have described. Canada's decisions in the next few years will be very important not only to us but to all those countries of the world that are looking for some breach in the wall that the people of the industrial nations are trying to build around themselves.
Before I embark upon a description of the other path and the course of action we can take if we are genuinely interested in this path, let me review recent trade tendencies in a very general and incomplete way. Generally speaking the western world has given lip service to multilateral trade, but in practice it has tended to group itself into regional groupings. We have the regional groupings of E.C.M., of EFTA, of South America and most recently of Africa. We have the Kennedy round of negotiations concerning GATT which in effect is an acceptance of the regional concept. This is one tendency, and I am afraid this regional tendency still stands in high favour in the minds of many of the economists in our western industrial nations who write articles to advise politicians.
On the other hand we still have those in the western nations who are putting up a fight for the multilateral principle, and in all fairness I think Canada under all governments has been consistent in advocating this principle even though a few years ago we heard in the house from the then opposition side great claims that we should enter into these regional blocs, that we should join these rich men's clubs and bar the door to the poor at our gates. Fortunately this phase did not last long, because so far as the general philosophy in Canada is concerned the multilateral side seems to be winning out.
Having given this general and incomplete history I should like to suggest now that the basis of the new path that could be considered is an attitude of mind. The attitude of mind is that there are two billion people in the world who at the present time do not play much of a role in world trade, certainly far less than 20 per cent, and this vast number of people who enjoy such a small percentage of world trade want a better living standard. They know they can only achieve a better living standard by trading with the rich industrial nations. They do not want to have to come to our door at GATT and plead for crumbs.
Canada, on the other hand, is not so rigidly bound by the fears of the past that crush the minds and spirits of leaders in 20220-562i
Supply-Trade and Commerce
western Europe. We still have a spark or two left in us that will pioneer a new course. But I say first of all that the attitude should be that the needs and wants of these people must be paramount, not our own. Let me give an example. In 1943 men of high principle enunciated the principle of a world food bank. It was not until 1961 that we got the world food bank program on its feet, and it is in action today. What caused that sudden reversal of the field in 1961? It was the declaration by those representing Canada at the world conference in Rome that we put the needs of these people first, that our thought was not just to get rid of surplus wheat or surplus something else but that what these people wanted they should have a right to. The practical way in which we did this, of course, was to offer to put cash into the fund, and we agreed that Canadian money could be used to buy food anywhere in the world. This won the support, not opposition, of the newly developing nations.
I could go on and talk about this at great length, but over and over again as I go through Hansard for the last year and a half I find the opposite attitude on the part of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think many of us who tried so hard to sell Canadian wheat must have been shocked at the answer of the minister just yesterday to the question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia. With regard to the failure of crops in Europe the minister said, as found on page 8837 of Hansard:
-I am satisfied that if these reports are correct- and I hope they are from the point of view of Canadian wheat prospects-we shall get our full share of the business that is going.
This is my point, Mr. Chairman. If you are going to be a good salesman of wheat, if you are going to be a person who helps these countries get on their feet, you will only succeed if your attitude is right; namely that you want to help them because in helping them you will always help yourself. This is the key to the path that in my opinion will lead to the bringing of all these people into the trade picture in the world of today.
What are some of these trading techniques? Some are old and some are new. Some may be proven no good, but at least we should take a look at them. From the questions I have asked in the last year and a half the minister knows that I am tremendously interested in international commodity agreements. Generally speaking there are two classes of international commodity agreements. The first

Supply-Trade and Commerce class comprises those between the traditional traders of the world, hard headed and experienced people who can look after themselves. They establish a minimum and a maximum and trade within those two limits.
But there is a new type of international commodity agreement yet to be developed and which must be developed if we are going to break the barrier between the newly developing nations and the industrialized nations. These newly developing countries need to accept the fact that we in the rich countries of the world recognize and want them to join, not to take away their shirts and their livelihood from them by grinding them down to the lowest possible prices, but by deliberately going out to raise and double their prices.
Most of these countries are producers of staple products. These are all they have got to sell and we could double their basic income, and it would not mean very much to us at the retail level. In that way we could give them a chance to buy the things they need from us. This is the way you can move forward; but you have to have the attitude.
We can remember the debates and questions we had last year on an international sugar agreement. I went through the record again this morning and I should like to give one quotation which shows a classic example of the attitude that exists in Canada, and in particular in the minister's mind. Everyone knows why there is not a sugar agreement today, because of the dispute between the United States and Cuba, but this is what the minister said in one of his answers:
I am of the opinion that it would be unwise at the moment to enter into long term agreements with commonwealth suppliers or any other suppliers.
And further on he said:
-until the market has settled down before we commit ourselves to any long term contract which would oblige Canadian consumers to pay higher prices in the long run.

We know that because of the energy and natural resources available to us we can manufacture automobiles and many steel products cheaper than it can be done in the United States. We have all the basic ingredients of success in this field. Why does not United States capital come in to build the plants? The reason is obvious: They never know what their own government is likely to do when they try to send their products back into the United States. The Americans know they are likely to run out of iron by 1975 or 1980, not taking into account the new finds of ore in Alaska. They would like access to our stable supplies of iron. We could supply them part of our iron for the next 30 or 40 years and guarantee them a suitable deal. We, in return, want a faster growth rate in processing than we have at present. At the beginning, progress is slow but over the years the percentage climbs and we can visualize in 20, 30 or 40 years, equality with our neighbour. Why should there not be that equality? We have the energy and we have the resources. The capital will certainly move around, provided we get rid of the present Minister of Finance. Given equality in taxes and the movement of money we could hold our own with any country in the world; we could move into the world pattern with lower costs and a better chance of selling. If any hon. member doubts this, let him read the Paley report in the United States of 1952, and the


latest report entitled "Resources for America's Future" dated in April, 1963.
I have to agree with the minister that we must go all out and negotiate in GATT- the biggest bargaining table over pennies the world has ever seen. But to me, coming from an agricultural background, it is like putting your best hired hand to milking a dried out cow: You must put him on it because it is very difficult to get milk out of her. But look around and you can see miles of green pastures full of heifers newly freshened. That is where the milk is. Let us get cracking and go where the milk is.
I could go on to deal with a lot of other related matters but I think I have made my point.

I followed the remarks of the previous speaker with a great deal of interest. I was much taken by his down to earth approach. The hon. member is one whom I consider as being a countryman with a lot of common sense in his attitude. He demonstrated this when he was a minister in the former government. However, I must be very careful before saying any more in that direction.
I do want to say I appreciate the courtesy shown by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when dealing with questions I have brought to his attention. I recognize his ability and keenness-and when an old socialist says that of a man who is, ultimately, a free enterpriser, he is going a long way. But I give credit where it is due from my point of view, and I recognize also the good work the officials of the department have been doing both in Canada and abroad.
From correspondence I have received and from what I know, I think everything possible should be done to upgrade the importance of our trade commissioners overseas in their dealings with countries abroad and with private interests in those countries. I think that throughout the years there has been a tendency in some quarters to look upon trade commissioners in the same way as my mother looked upon shopkeepers, that is, to feel they were not as important as were some other people. I do think everything should be done to upgrade the importance of our trade commissioners, in view of the great value of their work to the Canadian economy.
Before proceeding to make a few other remarks on the subject of trade I wish to say that I support wholeheartedly the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Dan-

forth, particularly with regard to the need for a department of consumers. I trust the minister will give those suggestions serious consideration because I know that coming from a member of this group they were made on a strictly non-partisan basis in the best interests of all concerned.
I was particularly interested in his reference to the necessity for "truth in packaging" legislation. We were told that such legislation is in effect in the United States and I think it is greatly to be desired. Only two or three days ago a clock came into my hands. It had been sold or given away in return for coupons by the I.G.A. stores in Ottawa. This clock came enclosed in a carton about eight inches by 15 inches and in large letters across the side of the carton the words "Made in Canada" appear. The letters are at least an inch high. But if you take the clock out of the carton and look closely, in letters you almost have to use a microscope to read, on the bottom of the clock, appear the words "made in the United States". I think this is thoroughly dishonest packaging, and I believe there should be some legislation to protect the Canadian consumer against this type of deceit. This instance was brought to my attention by a consumer in Ottawa who was most indignant, because at the time of the transaction he thought he was getting a clock made in Canada.
I wish to make a few observations about our trade balance with Great Britain and the prospect of improving it from the point of view of the British as well as ourselves. We all realize the situation which exists with regard to our trade deficit, our deficit balance in dealings with the United States. The reverse is the case with regard to our balance of trade with the United Kingdom. I have always been of the opinion that we could do more in this respect, not in a large scale way but particularly with reference to the products and services which smaller organizations have to sell.
Because of my interest in this aspect I did inquire into what had been the result of a venture made by a relatively small company, compared with the large corporations we have in this country, which had come to Canada after being interested by some of our officials years ago. I am referring particularly to Gestetner (Canada) Ltd. I believe there is a possibility of interesting larger numbers of this type of British firm to locate in Canada. The activities of this company have been of great benefit to the Canadian economy since
Supply-Trade and Commerce their arrival. I want to bring to the minister's attention that this company came to Canada, after the possibilities of the market were directed to their attention by some of our people, in November, 1924. They formed a Canadian subsidiary of the English company and opened a small store, I understand, in Toronto. Then they began plans for selling in the eastern Canadian market, and later throughout the whole of Canada. They have expanded until at the present time they have 19 branches operating in Canada and a staff of over 500 people. These employees are concerned with direct sales and service amounting in Canada alone to over $3J million.
All these Gestetners are imported from Great Britain; they are sold in Canada and they are serviced in Canada. This company has continually expanded because it sells an excellent product. But the point is, Mr. Chairman, that all the profits of this company have been plowed back in reinvestment in Canada, which I think is the sort of thing that assists the Canadian economy. I know that in terms of the very large companies dealing with our natural resources, and so on, this is not a large company; but I do think there is an opportunity to interest more of these companies in Great Britain to establish similar branches in Canada in order to assist the British people with the marketing of their goods and to lessen the gap, shall I say, between our sales to Great Britain and our purchases from Great Britain.
The company has had excellent relationships with its employees; it has an excellent pension plan, and so on. Its policy is to sell first class products and provide first class service, to plow all the profits back into expansion in this country and the improvement of the firm's operations. As the result of this policy, this company which started in 1924 is worth over 200 times what it was at that time.
I give this one illustration, Mr. Chairman, because I was interested in seeing how this type of company developed in Canada and what possibilities there were for the development of similar companies. I do urge the minister and his officials to give some consideration to cultivating particularly what I consider to be a fertile field in this direction, because the British manufacturers produce some very excellent products, in many respects similar to those produced by the company I have mentioned, namely Gestetner (Canada) Ltd.

I have some very brief comments to make in connection with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I especially want to raise a point mentioned yesterday, or Tuesday more precisely, by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) with respect to sanctions some American groups would like to see imposed on the Canadian aluminum industry so that it would not be as competitive on their markets as it is now.
I raise this point because I consider that the aluminum industry needs, just as any other sector of industry, a reasonable measure of assistance from the Canadian government. The day before yesterday, when this question was raised, the minister answered rather briefly and said that the government had made representations to the American authorities on this matter. He did not use exactly these words, but when asked the following question:
Has the government made representations to the government of the United States regarding proposed changes in tariff duties on certain classes of aluminum products imported into Canada?
He answered:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
I feel, consequently, that this government is aware of the problem which we face at the present time and has made recommendations in this respect. The minister must be aware of the importance it has for the Canadian economy particularly in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia where those aluminum plants are located. In the Saguenay area particularly, if there were some kind of embargo or an increase in tariff on aluminum products exported to the United States, it would be a harsh blow for the economy of my area, since for all practical purposes the Saguenay area relies almost exclusively on the aluminum and pulp and paper industries to keep up its economy.
I believe our minister of commerce gets through a lot of work, but when he speaks later, I should like him to tell us what he has done to prevent the Americans from carrying out this threat against the aluminum industry of Canada.
He will have to take into consideration that this Canadian company is probably our largest international company, and I believe that we are justified in being proud of it since it has subsidiaries in almost every part of the world. It acts as a very good ambassador for Canada abroad, through the

exchanges of its Canadian personnel and that of its subsidiaries all over the world.
I believe it does a very good job, which promotes better understanding between the various countries and automatically helps to restore the economy of some countries. I have in mind the facts I personally witnessed while working for Alcan, where numerous engineers from underdeveloped countries were also working to complete their technical know-how and to go back later to their own countries in order to operate Alcan plants there. I think it is the duty of the minister, and mine also, to raise this point.
Should that come about, it would deal a heavy blow to the Canadian economy; to our trade balance with the United States, since 60 per cent of Alcan's sales of semi-fabricated aluminum products go to the United States, representing about $1 million annually. Surely the minister sees the danger and I hope he will do everything he can to make necessary representations in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Hamilton) dealt a moment ago with the problem of the automobile industry. I would like to go one step further and discuss the problem facing the Canadian automobile industry and arising out of the control of that industry by American parent companies.
Last year this government through the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) introduced a program to increase the percentage of parts made in Canada and going into the manufacture of automobiles. But, in my opinion, we have before us a glaring example of the urgent need to rapidly increase the percentage of parts going into the manufacture of automobiles sold in Canada. What we need in Canada is automobile parts which are 100 per cent made in Canada.
There is a strike going on at the plants of General Motors in the United States and we find that Canadian subsidiaries of that company in Oshawa are also affected. As a matter of fact, it is reported in the press today that more than 5,000 Canadian workers are now idle because of a shortage of parts on the assembly lines. I think that is conclusive evidence of the growing need for the Canadian automobile industry to become 100 per cent Canadian and, therefore, independent from the United States industry.
In the past some Canadian industries were denied the right to export their products to other countries because they had to yield to the policy dictated to them by the American parent company. I think the Americans are

quite wrong in maintaining such a situation in the automobile industry, because to my mind they should realize that the Canadian market is now large enough to justify 100 per cent Canadian production and the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce who are in close contact with their American opposite numbers should strive to make them accept the Canadian point of view and realize that such a situation, to a certain extent, is the cause of some of the prevailing grievances against the Americans.
While the United States is a very powerful neighbour that we respect they must also respect our country's economy and in allowing such a situation to prevail in Canada, I think they are doing a disservice, not only to their own country, but also to Canada. If the Americans wish to maintain in Canada manufacturing plants under their control, they will have to allow them to export to the United States without cost. Indeed, I trust that the agreement the Canadian government is hoping to sign with the American government in order to remove tariff barriers on Canadian exports to the United States will be a success and, as far as I am concerned, I would support the complete removal of such tariff barriers between Canada and the United States.
I admit that some industries will perhaps be affected, but on the other hand, I am aware of the fact that this would help the establishment of many other industries which would be able to expand and be more competitive on the American market.
Mr. Chairman, there is also another matter I wanted to discuss. I have in mind the publicity that the Department of Trade and Commerce is supposed to give to Canadian products.
We all know that the Department of Trade and Commerce is very much interested in the sale of wheat. Of course, it is important for the department to do so, because wheat is a most important product. It is interesting to note that we can ship this product abroad and have Canadians take advantage of the operation, but on the other hand there are other sectors of Canadian industry which need help. I wonder if the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce strive as hard to find markets for farm produce other than wheat.
For instance, we have the problem with respect to cheese production. That industry is now faced with a rather difficult problem, especially in eastern Canada.
For many years farm production in eastern Canada was looked upon as limited to dairy
Supply-Trade and Commerce products used in the manufacture of powdered milk and cheese.
In my opinion, it is a mistake to a certain extent, to force our farmers to change their type of production, ostensibly because there is no longer any market for the kind of dairy production in which they were engaged in the past.
As a matter of fact, there is a great deal of evidence in support of the contention that the demand for dairy products will be increasing, like that for all other products, for that matter and I believe that we must promote the dairy industry so as to provide for the needs which will increase proportionately.
In my opinion the Department of Industry should strive to find and secure a market for Canadian cheese in various countries. I know that England is one of our good customers as far as Canadian cheese is concerned, but when we look into the possibility of producing this commodity we cannot but conclude that we have still a long way to go.
A great deal could be done to stabilize the farm industry in eastern Canada, if a market could be found for cheese and for other dairy products.
It is a well known fact that Canada produces a high quality cheese, and I am of the opinion that the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce should do the promotional work required. In a word, they should be the salesmen needed to find the markets required for this product.
Mr. Chairman, there is another point I would like to deal with. It has been discussed often, but for a while it seemed to have been overlooked. The problem with which this industry is faced is a very difficult one, inasmuch as this industry was established in Canada many years ago.
Several of our Canadian spinning-mills forgot or neglected over the years, to modernize and now they find it difficult to compete with the production of other countries, particularly of Japan.
The textile industry employs a great number of workers, and the federal government should grant it very special attention.
I know that the minister must take into account existing international agreements and that he must avoid protecting any individual mill, because that might inspire the leaders of the countries to which wa export to enforce certain restrictions.
But considering that the textile industry employs many workers, I think that it is an industry which especially deserves the minister's attention and when he or his officials

There are two major factors, in my opinion, which should be taken into consideration with regard to the identification of imported products. There is certainly a deficiency in that respect. If the Canadian people could more easily ascertain the origin -of the products, I think that with a proper educational campaign, they could be convinced to buy Canadian products instead of imported ones. Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in the debate on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I think it only fitting to refer to some of the remarks made by the member for Qu'Ap-pelle, the former minister of agriculture, who set out six points in reference to trade in this country which should be taken very seriously by the minister.
Perhaps I do not need to say this, because it has been said on many occasions, but Canada is always in the unique position of being a country with surpluses, whereas most countries of the world are countries with Shortages. Our problems are always related to surpluses, whether we are dealing with grain, petroleum or coal. At the present time, as well as in the past, we have difficulty competing in so far as our surpluses are concerned, and we must compete because without trade Canada would fail. I should like to direct my remarks particularly in respect of two industries in Alberta, which I am sure the minister has considered. I refer to the coal and petroleum industries.
I do not wish to spend much time talking about the coal industry in Alberta, because I


have spoken in this regard on several occasions in the House of Commons, but I do wish to point out several things. It is a well known fact that the production of coal in Alberta and throughout Canada is declining because of competition with the natural gas and other petroleum products industries. Canada has one eighth of the entire coal supplies of the world and there was a time in the history of this country when people in the coal industry felt we were exporting too much coal because we were likely to run short. I might say this is the same attitude now taken by a great many people in respect of the natural gas industry. I wonder what those people would say today about their attitude toward coal exports. On one other occasion I said that we in Canada went to bed with our coal, -and if we continue our present attitude we may well have to go to bed with some of the natural gas in this country.
For many years in Alberta I have advocated the export of not only coal but of natural gas. The only substantial market left in the world, as far as we are concerned, for the sale of our coal, is the Japanese market, and it is interesting to note that the only way we can maintain our position in the sale of coal to that market is by paying a subvention on the per ton shipment of coal. It must seem strange to individuals engaged in the coal industry that we have to use taxpayers' money to help this minor resource compete. There are two sides to that story. We must always remember that by paying a subvention we not only help this industry compete in world markets but also provide employment for miners.
The matter of coal subventions has been before parliament on several occasions and is the subject of a number of orders in council. Perhaps I may be allowed to review these for a moment. On December 5, 1939 the subvention on coal for sale to Japan was $1 per ton. In 1949 the subvention was $1 per ton. The subvention remained at $1 per ton until 1957 when, on July 22, it was increased to $2.25 per ton. On April 9, 1958 by order in council the subvention was increased to $4 per ton. In 1959 it was increased to $4.50 per ton. On April 2, 1962 the subvention was reduced to $3.50 per ton, and on October 25, 1962 it was further reduced to $3.15 per ton. One can readily see that subventions are necessary in respect of this industry, not only to assist it to compete, but to provide employment for miners. An increase in trade is naturally followed by an increase

in employment, but I am sure hon. members from the maritimes would agree with me that even during boom periods in the rest of Canada there is somewhat of a depression there and in other coal producing areas, because it is a seasonal industry.
We have been able to increase our coal exports to somewhere between 700,000 and 800,000 tons. Last year I think the export of coal increased to 845,000 tons while at the same time the subvention was lowered.
Mr. W. C. Whittaker, the president of the coal operators association of western Canada, suggested that the industry would benefit from a reduction in transportation costs. We have talked in this house a great deal about rail abandonment. I suggest that we must work through the Department of Transport, in conjunction with other departments, to organize our transportation facilities in such a way that transportation costs can be reduced. Mr. Whittaker made a speech last month at Lake Louise, Alberta, which was reported in the Calgary Herald, and I should like to refer briefly to that speech. He was referring, as I said earlier, to the reduction of transportation costs, and I am sure everyone will agree that if such a reduction was followed by a reduction in subventions on coal, it would be to the advantage of the coal operators of Canada and the taxpayers as a whole. In such event perhaps the coal industry in Canada would be able to compete with the Australian coal industry, which is one of the largest suppliers of coal to Japan. Mr. Whittaker said at Lake Louise that unless the present rate of $6 per ton cost for railroad transportation and ship loading was reduced to about $4.50, coal exports could well pass -out of the picture in Canada.
I should like to congratulate the minister upon his fair handling of subventions on coal. Everyone has paid him a compliment today about his opening remarks, and I should also like to be in that positive position. The export of coal from Canmore and the Crowsnest pass may well range this year from 900,000 to 1,000,000 tons. That increase in exports would create an increase in employment in those areas. Mr. Whittaker suggests that we must cut transportation costs from $6 per ton to $4.50 per ton. I remember when we not only exported more coal but used more coal for home consumption, and at that time the coal was being transported on mixed cargo trains. With our streamlined transportation industry of today coal is moved in trains strictly limited to the transportation of coal. I am sure the transportation industry would be
Supply-Trade and Commerce delighted by an increase in the production in coal transportation. Serious consideration should be given to some method of cutting costs of transportation so as to help the Canadian coal industry compete for the Japanese market, which would naturally be followed by an increase in the amount of coal transported by those railway companies.
When I was in Japan in 1958, with an industrial firm rather than in connection with my duties as a member of parliament, I was talking with one of the major steel manufacturers of that country who told me that the difference of 10 cents to 20 cents in the cost of coal per ton would have a serious effect on their decision as to where they would buy a particular kind of coking coal. Ten or 20 cents does not seem to be a great deal of money, but when exchanged for Japanese currency in Japan it is indeed something to be considered.
In this regard Australia has been able to outdo us in competing for the market and that is the reason we have had to keep the subvention as high as it has been. It was the Conservative government that established the subvention. The minister has admitted that many of these programs were initiated by the Conservatives and have been carried on by the present administration. When we established the subvention we opened up a market for this coal. They now know in Japan that we have good hard, bituminous coal mined in the mountains. Our quality and kind of coal can compete with any other kind of coal in the world. Therefore when we open up a market we can then cut down the subvention and cut down the cost to the taxpayer. So this does prove that this method is the way to open up avenues to get trade. Maybe this is what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle meant when he was dealing with those countries where they do not have as high a standard of living, and suggested that we should open up avenues of trade so that in future they will be able to compete with the more wealthy nations.
So the first recommendation is that we have to take a hard look at costs. The coal operators themselves cannot do anything about transportation costs. They can do something about the costs of mining. I might say to the minister, and I do not say this in too critical a way, that when I first went to the Canmore area in the foothills of the Rocky mountains, and right in the Rocky mountains, unemployment was rampant everywhere. Up to that time this coal had been used by the railways, but with auto-

When you think that in one coal area of Alberta there were 20 mines at one time, I believe, and today there are only two left you can see the importance of this matter.
Once again, with the scientific developments that are taking place and the byproduct commodities that may be made out of coal we never know when coal will become more important. It is well within the imagination, and I said this eight or nine years ago I believe, that some day coal will be processed at the minehead, piped like natural gas across the country and will compete with natural gas. Nylon stockings and many other things can be made out of coal and I say the coal industry is a long way from dead. During the period of transformation this government, because it is their responsibility just as it was our responsibility when we were in office, has to keep these mines operating. We assumed the responsibility of keeping them alive and, if Mr. Whittaker is right, unless we can cut the transportation costs it is impossible to compete even with the subsidy as it is today.

That is true, off the docks. As I pointed out, one of the great steel producers of Japan said that a difference of 10 or 15 cents a ton decides where they will buy this product. The minister may run into something I have encountered when he goes to Alberta. He will find that our Social Credit friends will stand on the platform- I see they have looked up immediately-and they will blame-I cannot use the word in the house I should like to use-all governments because we import coal into Canada.
I got the latest figures today from the coal board, and in 1963-64 we imported 13,880,000 tons of coal. When the Conservatives came into office Canada was importing some 20 million tons of coal. I think that is correct because I have made speeches on that point before.
Because of the policies implemented in the maritimes and, of course-I want to be fair in this regard-because of the competition of natural gas in the large urban centres of eastern Canada we have been able to cut down our coal imports. But there is one great fiction always uttered in western Canada and you have to explode it at least once a year before it gets away on you. The Social Cred-

iters will stand on the platform, especially in the soft coal areas where people are out of work, and blame everybody but themselves. The former minister of labour came to speak in my riding and he said that the worst thing he had ever seen was the living conditions in the East Coulee, Rosedale and Nacmine areas around Drumheller. He said he had never seen worse poverty than in this soft coal mining area.
These Social Crediters send speakers down there and they say that Canada is importing coal and that is the reason the miners are out of work. This is a fiction. The coal we bring into Canada is hard bituminous coal and the coal that is mined in the Drumheller valley is sub-bituminous, soft coal which is not suitable to be used for the same purpose for which the imported coal is used. The coal mined at Canmore and the coal mined in Nova Scotia are similar in energy and quality. This kind of fiction probably wins votes at the right time, but it causes a lot of headaches which people have to try to iron out afterwards. I believe this myth has now been exploded but I have heard it on many platforms. That particular coal is domestic coal and is not the kind of coal I am talking about.
I want to complete my remarks in that regard. We in Alberta are interested in the export of coal to Japan. We are interested in the export of coal from the Canmore and Crowsnest areas. A subvention was necessary to open that market, and to be able to keep it we must cut transportation and loading costs wherever we can. I would ask the minister to give this matter serious thought. If he really desires, and I believe he does, to carry out the important program in this regard that was started by the Conservative government, this is one thing that must be looked into if the program is going to survive.
I want to say something about another industry which is in competition with coal. I suppose one might say it is very difficult to talk about both industries at the same time when they are in competition with one another, but we have to be realists. They are in competition, and I must say that in many ways the natural gas industry has been able to undercut the costs of the coal industry, and that is one of the reasons for the problems of the coal industry.
I am glad to see that the minister does not belong to that school of thought-I know he does not-that used to prevail in Alberta, the Prowse school of thought under which the provincial Liberals at that time opposed the export of any natural gas because they

Private Bills
were frightened there would not be enough for use in the foreseeable future, or enough today. The Conservatives set up the national energy board, and I want to say something about that.
If I may review the situation first, up to 1957, I believe, very little natural gas was exported. One of the promises in the 1957 election which I heard the Leader of the Opposition make was that when elected the Conservatives would set up a national energy board. That promise was kept. It was a good promise and a good program. It is interesting to note that in 1959 we exported to the United States $16.5 million worth of natural gas. In 1960 it increased to $22.9 million, in 1961 to 40.6 million, in 1962 to $87.5 million, and in 1963 it almost reached the $100 million mark, or $93.8 million. The departmental officials have projected the increase. I know I am not breaking any confidence because they are always available to give expert advice if you seek it. I have had the best of cooperation from the experts in these departments. The officials hope that it will increase by another 9 per cent.
What does all this mean? With the imbalance of trade between the United States and Canada, and still worse the imbalance of dollars between our two countries, this dramatic step in exporting gas has helped bring about a balance of payments. The Department of Trade and Commerce alone cannot solve the problem, but with proper government policy, and working in conjunction with the Minister of Finance, every means of encouragement should be given to those people who form companies to build pipe lines to export natural gas, from Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia or whatever other area produces it.
The Borden commission was set up by the previous government, and from it and the reports emanating from the department, and from the Canada Year Book we have learned we have enough guaranteed natural gas in Canada for energy uses, not only for industry but also for domestic use during the next 30 years. If we continue to export it and if the Canadian consumer market increases, then of course we will get more exploration. At present exploration is taking place in the Northwest Territories where there have been some large findings, and now that the C.C.F. government has been defeated in Saskatchewan some natural gas may come to light that has been kind of tapped off in secret from the public.
