subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are discussing Bill No. S-27, an act respecting The Bell Telephone Company of Canada and the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) to the effect that if five new directors were added to the Bell Telephone Company, three would be appointed by the federal government.

Private Bills
I consider the amendment to be very sensible. Seventeen would be appointed by the shareholders and three by the government.
Some members may ask why should the government intervene? Needless to say it is not a matter of nationalizing the Bell Telephone Company, for in that case I would object for several reasons. First of all, I must say that the Bell Telephone Company is giving good service to the Canadian citizens at the present time. Anybody who wishes to have a phone can get it and in no time at all. The rates are not too high, except perhaps in the case of long distance calls. Moreover, I see two great benefits deriving from the fact that the Bell Telephone Company is a private enterprise. First, its services are tax-free, as far as the people are concerned. We are accustomed to the deficits, often substantial ones, shown by the majority of the crown companies and which are at the expense of the taxpayers. I suggest then that to have a nation-wide telephone service, available to everybody, and not requesting subsidies from the government to finance their deficit at the end of the year, is something of a tremendous value to Canadians.
The second advantage, and not the least, is that at the end of the year, not only does the company not request subsidies, but it pays taxes which fill the federal treasury and enables the government to earmark more money for social security, hospitalization insurance, family allowances and old age pensions. Naturally, we should be even more pleased if we knew this money was not being spent as interest on the debt; but in any event, I have mentioned two great advantages which make it clear why the Bell Telephone Company of Canada should not be nationalized, or handed over to the state. We have seen many cases where, as soon as a company is nationalized, deficits begin to accumulate; red tape and bureaucracy take over, and we are strongly against it.
But if three members were then appointed by the government, the majority of the directors could still continue to administer the company in a normal way, that is, to make profits. We have no objections to that because, any Canadian citizen who has money available for investment, like some members of this house probably have, may invest it in companies such as the Bell Telephone Company or a pulp and paper mill company and thus assist in developing the country.
Canadian citizens should be able to invest money in their national companies and help to develop their country. If there are profits
[Mr. Grtgoire.l
at the end of the year, the shareholders will draw dividends, and this will prompt other Canadian citizens to make investments in other similar Canadian companies. Every time Canadian citizens invest in Canadian companies, it is a good thing, because such companies foster the prosperity of the nation.
Therefore, there would still be seven directors to see to it that the Bell Telephone Company operates according to set standards, the three directors appointed by the government being there to see about protecting public interest. What is the public interest in a company such as the Bell Telephone? It may be thought of in terms of rates. The three government appointed directors would look after the public interest, and would make sure that telephone customers can get the best service possible with the least possible expense.
Would three directors appointed by the government have enough influence on the whole group of shareholders to enable them to look after the public interest in that field? At the present time there are 15 who are businessmen, directors, men of action. Hereafter, there would be five more, including two appointed by the shareholders and three by the government.
I am wondering if the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) would not have been better advised to raise that percentage, requesting that five out of 20 directors, or a quarter, be appointed by other people than the shareholders?
For instance, three of those directors could be appointed by the federal government, another one by the 10 Canadian provinces after reaching an agreement, or two might be appointed by the federal government and two by the ten provinces and a fifth one by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities since the municipalities form another public body; there are municipalities throughout Canada and they avail themselves of the Bell Telephone Company services.
If we increase by five the number of directors of that company, it seems to me that instead of suggesting action or a compromise as was done by the hon. member for Timiskaming, it would be more appropriate to suggest a good solution, by saying: These five new directors will be appointed on the following basis: two by the federal government, two by the ten provincial governments, after reaching an agreement, and one by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities.

In that case 25 per cent of the members of the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company would represent various public bodies. It would not amount to nationalization exactly but it might satisfy those who want better representation of public interest in a company of national importance, a company that has no competitors and, in fact, operates more or less as a monopoly.
In this type of company public interest would be more satisfactorily safeguarded if five rather than three members were appointed by the public bodies. Five out of 20 is equal to 25 per cent of the board of directors, whereas three out of 20 only amounts to 15 per cent.
So, instead of having three new directors appointed by the federal government, two would be appointed by the federal government, two by the provincial governments and one by the municipalities as a whole.
There would be then representatives from public organizations, at all levels, within a national company such as the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. This company is doing business throughout Canada on a non-competitive basis. The individual Canadian citizen, be he a member of parliament, a prime minister, an alderman or anyone else, has no choice between two companies. If there is only one set of telephone cables passing in front of your home or your office, you have to use them. In fact, there is no competition.
It is a good thing that some of the decisions taken by the directors of such a company be influenced by members of public organizations, but not entirely so, not even by a majority, for it has been proven that whenever a majority of businessmen are appointed directors of a company, we can be sure that the company is better managed than by government officials or bureaucrats.
That is why I intend to move an amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Timiskaming, to the effect that not three directors be appointed by the federal government but that five directors be appointed by various public agencies, namely, two by the federal government, two by the provincial governments and one by the union of municipalities. It is merely a matter of substituting the figure five to the figure three.
I think I pointed out that it was a good thing that the businessmen who at present manage the Bell Telephone Company of Canada continue to do so and hold a majority of the votes in the company. However, on the other hand, they would be assisted by 25 per cent of the directors who would rep-
Private Bills
resent the public and see to it that the interests of every Canadian be better safeguarded whenever a decision is taken.
Mr. Chairman, this seems to be a reasonable suggestion.
If the telephone company finds that 15 directors are not enough and wishes to increase their number, it means that the company has greatly expanded and is doing so much business that 15 directors will not suffice. We are therefore in agreement, since the company itself realizes that 15 directors are not enough to supervise its operations.
But the five directors are added to the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company, these five new directors will have to bring something new, something which does not exist at the present time within the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
It is true that there are businessmen, but representatives of the public interests are missing.
Working for a profit is not everything- it is the purpose of any business firm, of any concern-there ought to be some directors to see to it that the public interest is looked after. I am not saying that it is the case at the present time; maybe it is. But the public interest would still be better taken care of if five directors out of 20, or 25 per cent of the company's directors were appointed in a more specific manner in order to look after the public interest, two at the federal level as I suggested, two at the provincial level, and one at the municipal level.
Moreover, it would be possible to change this formula again. This is merely a suggestion. The school boards might also like to have a representative or a director on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company. In that case it might be possible to introduce a further subamendment in order to include a sixth director who would represent the various school boards in Canada. In this way all public bodies in the country would be represented. We would then be sure that the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada would better cover our citizens as a whole.
At the present time the board of directors of the company only represents the shareholders' interests. This is necessary, I admit, and we recognize that the majority of the directors must represent the shareholders. But we would also like to see all our public bodies represented in a company of this kind so that all points of view can be expressed within the board of directors.

Private Bills
If 20 directors are not enough, we are ready to increase the number beyond that figure so that everyone will be represented.
There is nothing-and I am sure that hon. members will agree on this point-there is nothing either to prevent labour unions also from the privilege of appointing a director to the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. Let us keep in mind that there are more than five million workers in Canada, five million wage-earners, most of whom are telephone users, and whenever they use the telephone they have no choice but to subscribe to the company whose cables run in front of their homes. Yet, when policy decisions are to be made, those people have no say in the matter.
Therefore, it would seem to me normal that the workers themselves be entitled to choose a representative on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company.
Therefore, before my time is up I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) the following:
that the figure "five" be substituted to the figure "three" in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
Thus, five members only of the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada will be appointed by public bodies. If this is not sufficient, more can be added, so that the federal and provincial governments, municipalities, school boards and labour unions be represented on the board.
The farmers should not be forgotten either, because, unfortunately, they have no say in the matter. And they are possibly the ones who suffer most from certain attitudes taken by the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
It is obvious that farm houses are more distant from one another than city houses, and that is why not all hamlets or farms in Canada have telephones. Now if farmers were represented on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, they would be in a position, they would be in a better position to suggest to the company that telephone service be provided, not only in towns, but also on farms across the country. I think that would be of benefit to a large segment of our population, that is the farmers, just as it would be a good thing to have a representative of the labour unions.
Let us not forget businessmen. If we go into a business office or a commercial establishment and look at its telephone account at the end of a month, we find that quite a few long distance calls have been

made, and that they run into quite a bit of money.
If the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada were to include a representative of every social class, those representatives might be in a position to suggest to the management various improvements, especially in the matter of long-distance charges.
The Bell Telephone Company of Canada would benefit in many ways if all classes of citizens in Canada were represented on its board of directors.
Even then, Mr. Chairman, I am overlooking some. If some unemployed worker were appointed director, perhaps might such a person, sitting on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, suggest that, during periods of unemployment, the unemployed should not be requested to pay their telephone bills. The unemployed need the telephone as much as anyone else. In cases of emergency, to call the hospital, the police or the fire department, they need the telephone service as much as any other class of society.
If there were an unemployed person on the board of directors of that company to suggest that an individual who is out of work should not have to pay his telephone bill, that again would be beneficial to society. It would be another benefit among all those which the Canadian people are getting from a company such as the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
I may have overlooked other benefits, but I begin to realize that for the Bell Telephone 20 directors would not be enough-

speechtext: I merely said, Mr. Chairman, that in essence it does not really matter whether it is three out of 20, or five out of 20, or four out of 20, or some other number or percentage around that figure. The principal point that we should concern ourselves with, which initially was raised by my colleague from Timiskaming and which we have been dealing with for many, many years as a political party, is that the general public should somehow or other have some say in the internal operations of a public service utility such as Bell Telephone.

Mr. Chairman, may I say that I believe that in committee of the whole I am entitled to speak again on this subject and to qualify my idea. I shall then explain further my opinion, for the benefit of the member for Skeena.
I agree with the hon. member for Skeena that it is not necessarily the figure three or the figure five that counts. What matters is the principle that there be also representatives of public bodies.
Private Bills
In my opinion-and I believe the hon. member for Skeena shares such views-there are many public bodies which would benefit from some representation within the Bell Telephone Company of Canada: the decisions taken might be improved and the interests of the various levels of society better protected.
I suggested five directors out of a total of 20, but perhaps I should have suggested even more, for I would also like someone to represent the federal government on the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. I just gave that figure as an example because the provinces and municipalities should also have a say at board meetings. In other words, the three levels of government should each have a representative. In addition, I should like the labour unions to have a representative and, as I said a moment ago, the farmers should also have a voice; they may be the class of people where one finds the highest proportion of citizens who are deprived of telephone service on account of the fact that farms are too far from one another.
I further stated that a director should speak for the unemployed since such a person could suggest that an unemployed subscriber should be exempted from paying his telephone bill during the time he is out of work.
Then, it requires more than the three directors mentioned by the hon. member for Timiskaming in his amendment. But I stated clearly that I want the majority of directors to be representatives of the shareholders of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, because they must administer the savings of those people. It must not become a state-controlled corporation, but remain a company managed by a majority of directors representing the shareholders.
However, it would be helpful to have, in addition, representatives of all public bodies so that they could bring forward their views, as well as those of all classes of Canadian society.

Mr. Chairman, the interesting thing about that question of privilege is that the member for Lapointe was smiling when he raised it, which would indicate that he is not really serious about my becoming enamoured of the philosophy espoused by his leader.
There is no doubt that members of parliament are concerned with making sure that the public interest is served, and that the public is assured that this company has its best interests in mind. I think the public should be provided with some mechanism by which it can take part in making policy decisions. I am sure the sponsor of this bill is vitally concerned with the public's interest. Perhaps I should remind the members of

this committee that the principles contained in the proposal we are now discussing were originally initiated by members of this party, which has always had the public's interest at heart. I am sure the Bell Telephone Company officials are concerned about public interest and want to make sure that the public is served in the best possible manner.
Perhaps this is an appropriate time for the sponsor of this bill to communicate to the officials of the Bell Telephone Company, if he has not done so already, that there is a growing concern, as far away as Halifax, about the operation of the Bell Telephone Company. He should perhaps concern himself with some method by which the general public could have representation on this board of directors. He may be well advised to communicate the fact that there is growing interest in parliament in respect of the operations of the Bell Telephone, and he may well ask those officials what they intend to do in this regard. Perhaps the sponsor of the bill should allow it to stand while the Bell Telephone Company officials consider the proposals which have been made, and perhaps meet with members of parliament who are interested in this matter in an attempt to find some compromise or arithmetical solution to the obvious differences.
It is easy for the member for Lapointe to say 25 per cent and that may be a good figure. It is equally easy for some other hon. member to say that he does not think it should be 25 per cent, that a more proper division would be 30 per cent or 26 per cent, or six members, or some other ratio of members of the board of directors selected by the governor in council and appointed to represent the public interest, compared with those appointed by the company under the normal rules of corporation activity.
In this discussion with the Bell Telephone Company we might reach an agreeable figure. After all, in something of this nature I do not think anybody wants to say to Bell Telephone or any other public utility: This is what we think is a proper ratio, 25 per cent appointed by the governor in council and 75 per cent selected at the annual meetings of the company in the way it is normally done. I do not even think we should say arbitrarily, as was suggested by the hon. member for Timiskaming initially, that three out of the 20 should be appointed by the governor in council. What percentage that would be I could not say. It is around 15 per cent. This

is just as arbitrary a figure as the 25 per cent suggested by the hon. member for Lapointe.
I think a far more reasoned and reasonable approach would be to communicate with the Bell Telephone Company through the sponsor of the bill and indicate our wishes to them so that we can arrange to sit down and talk about the matter in an informal way. Of course, whatever figure we arrive at, it also will be arbitrary. Unless we had a board of directors numbering 1,000 I do not think we could possibly have representation for all sections of the economy and all groups of subscribers. But some balance should be sought and there should be acceptance of the idea that if one person is appointed by the union of B.C. municipalities, for the sake of argument, it will be generally understood this is fair enough representation of that particular group of people. If we agree that the people working for the company should have some representation, it may also be possible that one such person will be sufficient to represent that block of people. And so on down the line.

Mr. Chairman, when we recessed I was speaking about the report of natural gas, and I would like to conclude that phase of my remarks by saying that at present there are two applications before


the provincial bodies which will likely come before the national energy board. One is an application for trans-Canada allotment in the Alberta southern system, and in my remarks before the evening recess I said the Borden commission, the reports of the petroleum industry itself, and the Canada Year Book all have indicated we have sufficient natural gas and proven reserves to enable us to export natural gas from Canada which would help us with our imbalance of trade with the United States, and our imbalance of dollars.
Everything possible should be done to encourage companies that are in the pipe line business, and to provide assistance for them in the tax structure so that we can help the flow of Canadian dollars into our own industry. I question, and I am sure the minister would question also, whether there is a single company in Canada today owning crude petroleum supplies, or natural gas or any of its by-products that is not probably 70 per cent controlled by foreign capital, irrespective of what the Minister of Finance may have said in the past. In fact Canadian Oil, B.A. and some of those other companies that were true Canadian companies have recently passed into the hands of foreign control; but if a little more encouragement were provided in the tax structure for Canadian companies, then Canadians with savings would be prompted to put their savings into investments in Canadian companies and syndicates.
The national oil policy is one which was devised by the Conservative government. The eastern market in Canada gets its oil supplies from Venezuela and other countries, but we know that the oil producing companies in those countries are financed with United States money, so naturally the Americans are interested in that supply of oil coming into what we call the Montreal market. Naturally we have to work out details with the United States on such markets, and it was during the term of office of the Conservative government that a very good deal was worked out on a three year basis. I want to drive that point home, because today the authorities are working such negotiations out on a year to year basis.
Everybody who has experience in the oil industry knows that after the Suez crisis was over the demand for Canadian crude oil, particularly crude oil from western Canada, fell off, and it was necessary to hold talks and conferences with the United States on the problem; and it was by getting into the United States western market that we were able to improve the market for Canadian crude oil. For example, as I said earlier this

afternoon, in 1960 we were able to export about 113,000 barrels of crude per day, and because of our national oil policy and the deal which we worked out with the United States, in 1963 we were able to export into the United States market 248,000 barrels per day.
I would ask the minister to remember that when this deal was made by the then minister of trade and commerce, Hon. George Hees, the petroleum industry was very happy with it. This industry appreciates the problems in reference to the imports of crude into the eastern market. It appreciates the problem that if there were quotas put on the eastern market it might increase the cost here and, moreover, might cause trouble in those countries from which the oil is coming. It might cause the kind of trouble and create the kind of philosophy which neither Canada nor the United States wants.
In this regard the United States worked out a compromise involving its western market on a three year basis. We said we would try to increase our exports to 250,000 barrels of crude a day and hoped to raise it to a level of 800,000 barrels a day. I think the minister can take some pride in the fact that in 1963 we almost hit that target by producing 786,000 barrels per day for home and export consumption. However, I am told by petroleum men in Calgary that now, instead of a three year target they have only a one year target, and this has led to a new development in Montreal where a new refinery extension has been built for B.A. Oil.
The reason for this is that with this one year target, or one year deal with the United States, they feel the market might fall off, and so they have built an extension to their refinery in order to refine an extra 25,000 barrels of foreign crude a day. There is anxiety among people in the oil and petroleum industry in western Canada about this one year deal, and I urge that our efforts should be bent, as they were when the national oil policy was announced, to having a three or five year plan. By so doing we will not have the kind of development which will continue to encourage imports into this country, thus creating greater imblance of trade and imbalance of dollars between Canada and the United States. When we talk about currency in this country let us face the fact that if you go overseas, whether you buy pounds sterling or dollars you pay for them in United States dollars. They control the markets. We listened to the suggestions made today by my hon. friend from Qu'Ap-
Supply-Trade and Commerce pelle. If we are to be a mature country we should set up the proper institutions internationally so that we would be dealing in Canadian dollars as well as in United States dollars. Then we could talk. Then we could trade and then we could sell in world markets. The oil industry is prospering in Canada today, due to the national oil policy implemented by the former government. I know the present minister is going along with that policy. I will go further. I will congratulate him and the officials of his department on going ahead with it. As a result of that national policy we were able in 1963 to produce 786,000 barrels of crude per day compared with 462,000 barrels in 1958. When I say "produce" I mean production in the sense that consumers at home and in the export market are using that amount, and this spells dollars for Canada. I say that the oil industry is one of the most important industries in Canada today, along with agriculture, and that its prosperity or otherwise affects the whole of our economy.
We heard today an enlightened speech by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I went along with him in his six points. He was enthused. I am sure the minister was really interested. But it seems to me that when we are discussing the building up of trade with countries having a lower standard of living than our own we should begin to take a hard look at our relations with China. We have made wheat deals with China and we have made oil deals. There may be other deals in store. If we are going to trade with a country of 600 million people the Department of External Affairs should take a look at the situation because if we deal with these people by selling them goods we may have to deal with them otherwise. It seems to me that as the parties change places in this house, officials of the department continue to advise and curb the ministers to whom they are responsible. I can speak freely because I am in opposition. I believe it is time that Canada, in spite of what the United States may do, should recognize China as a country. Remember, there are six or seven hundred million human beings there and they cannot be ignored. We are a country of 19 million people and we are sitting on surplus resources. We have reserves of wheat, natural gas, petroleum, iron ore; we have a surplus of everything. Can we continue to hold these resources for 19 million people unless, first of all, we begin recognizing the countries we must deal with and, in the second place, we begin to change the archaic and out of date

Supply-Trade and Commerce rules which govern immigration into this country? You cannot have one without the other. If there is to be peace in the world we have to show ourselves as businessmen of good will.

The hon. member for Bow River said he could speak freely because he was in the opposition. I also intend to speak freely tonight. What I say does not involve the government in any way; nor it is necessarily in line with government policy.
I want to talk about energy and more particularly about our trade in energy. I should like first, however, to congratulate the minister. The last time he brought his estimates forward we congratulated him because he was a new minister. This time we are all congratulating him on the tremendous performance of his department. Certainly he has shown great qualities in leadership with respect to our very successful trade drive.
One of the best tests of what is happening to our economy is our balance of payments. Three years ago our expenditures abroad were far in excess of our earnings and we had a balance of payments deficit of roughly $1.5 billion. It has now been reduced to half a billion. This improvement is one measure of the government's accomplishments in the field of foreign trade. It is of interest to all of us, not only in respect to trade, but in respect to foreign ownership in Canadian enterprises.
In the energy field there has been a remarkable improvement. At the end of world war II we were importing two thirds of our fuel. The bulk of it came from the United States, but some oil came from Venezuela. Today we are approaching a balance. We are, roughly, 70 per cent self-sufficent in respect to oil. We are more than self-sufficient with respect to hydro power and natural gas. We are still importing some coal. But, over-all we are 90 per cent self-sufficient in respect to energy. The progress made in this field is

one of the reasons why the affairs of this nation are in much better shape today than they were a few years ago.
Our changing pattern of trade reflects Canada's changing patterns of fuel consumption, in particular the tremendous increase in the importance of oil. Now it accounts for 60 per cent of our consumption of energy, having risen from 20 per cent. We are using more oil than anything else. Oil and gas together supply roughly three quarters of our energy requirements. Wood has almost disappeared as a source of energy and the importance of coal has declined not only in relative but also in absolute terms.
All over the world we are witnessing this progressive shift from what we thought to be the more durable forms of energy to the more exhaustible forms such as oil and natural gas. This shift is a matter of great concern to many people. Today oil is on the crest of the wave, so to speak. It accounts for 40 per cent of all world trade at the present time. Ten billion dollars worth of oil moves between nations annually on this globe of ours, but this increasing volume of
011	is being recovered in the context of increasing reserves. In the world today, if not a single additional exploratory well were drilled, there is still 40 years of supply at the current rates of consumption. On this continent, where oil has been in extensive use for over a century, there are still about
12	to 15 years supply. This 12 to 15 year figure frightens some people, and yet if one goes back over the past century he finds that there has been a 10 or 15 years supply proven out and available at any one point of time. The reason this has happened is that the oil industry has found it necessary to have something which you might call a working inventory in the order of 10 to 15 years supply on hand. It does not pay the industry to find too much oil, and consequently the industry keeps a limited amount of proven oil ahead of itself. It has been drilling deeper and using new techniques, and the proven oil reserves have mounted roughly in line with the immense increase in consumption on this continent.
Going overseas, mankind has found even greater quantities of this energy. In the world today there is at least as much natural gas, physically speaking at least, as there is oil; yet the consumption of natural gas lags behind that of oil by a considerable margin. In many parts of the world natural gas is hardly used at all. Even in Canada it is largely a post-war phenomenon. So if oil 20220-563
Supply-Trade and Commerce were to show some signs of exhaustion, natural gas is coming along behind it. Again, behind natural gas and oil are these tremendous quantities of bituminous sands, oil shales and the like. For example, we have in northern Alberta alone more oil in the form of tar sands than has been found in the entire world in conventional oil pools. So we have a larger oil inventory in the form of tar sands than we have oil and gas in the conventional sense.
Then of course we have coal. We have coal in vast amounts, hence the prospect that the alarmist sees only a decade or two away, that of making synthetic oils and gases from coal, could utilize the pipe lines through which oil and gas now move to market. This possibility has been there for a long time. In the 1860's in the United States when oil was beginning to be used extensively for lighting lamps, greasing wheels, and so on, there was concern amongst the conservationists of that day who were saying there was only 10 to 15 years of proven oil left in the ground. They said, "What will we do?" The chemists of that day said, "We can turn to synthetic oils and gases made from coal". That was 100 years ago. Technology was on the horizon then, and it is on the horizon now. Its promise may still be 50 years away. So we may not want alternative forms of energy, including the production of synthetic oil and gas from coal, for a long time to come.
We have hydro power. In the world perhaps 5 per cent of the hydro resources are developed. On this continent only about 40 per cent have been harnessed. In Canada an even smaller percentage has so far been utilized, and in a province like British Columbia only 10 per cent has been put to work. In other words, there are immense quantities of hydroelectric power available and it will become increasingly available as water is developed for other uses and as its multipurpose applications make power in effect a by-product of water for industrial purposes, agricultural, human consumption, and so on. Behind all this we have nuclear energy. We have tremendous amounts of uranium, thorium, and resources of that kind.
The concern about energy, in other words, has evaporated over the last 20 years. It is no longer a matter of whether mankind will run out of energy; it is now a matter of which is the cheapest of a number of alternative sources. We are tending to concentrate today on the more exhaustible forms of energy like oil and gas, but we know we can

Supply-Trade and Commerce turn to the tar sands, the oil shales, to coal and eventually to the nuclear sources of energy. It is merely a matter of cost. And today costs are coming down; we know they are not out of reach. Hence we are likely to see some important applications of nuclear energy within the next decade or two.
So supply is not really a problem. This has a very important implication, if true. It means that a country like Canada that has abundant sources of energy can trade with some confidence; that it does not have to worry about keeping all its forms of energy at home.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTION TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question? During the last two or three years has the hon. member always been in favour of exporting all types of energy from Canada, particularly in the case of natural gas and electrical energy-I am thinking particularly of the Columbia river-from Canada to the United States? Has the hon. member always taken that position?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTION TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Yes, I have always felt that we could export energy, with proper safeguards. We can export energy if we do not export it at prices lower than Canadians have to pay. We should not export our lowest priced energy to neighbouring areas of consumption. But I would say that we should be prepared to trade, as long as there is an advantage in financial terms of that trade.
Another test of the availability of energy is its price; that is, the price of energy compared with other things. The delivered price has been tending to fall not only in Canada but, generally speaking, throughout the world. Therefore, when the price test is applied, I suggest that energy is becoming more abundant. Delivered costs are coming down even more rapidly than the cost at the source of the energy, because the means of transportation have been very much improved, the oil pipe line is very much more efficient than the gas pipe line-it is three or four times more efficient than the gas pipe line-and the gas pipe line is several times more efficient than moving coal by rail.
Coal can only be moved a few hundred miles in comparison with oil, which can be moved thousands of miles. In other words, oil can move much further from its source to its market: it can move halfway around the world. Natural gas can move across a continent and still be competitive; but coal can move only a few hundred miles and be competitive. It should really be consumed at its point of origin.

These are among the facts of life that the long term forecasts reveal, and long term planning in the freest or most indicative sense indicates this is the most sensible way of managing the energy resources of a region or a nation. Basically we are seeing a lowering of the ceiling on the price of energy because of these improved means of transportation, increased availabilities and more efficient utilization. The average thermal power plant 50 years ago was only 15 per cent efficient; today it is 30 per cent efficient. Recent discoveries are suggesting efficiencies of better than 50 per cent. So much more of the energy delivered to a given point is being utilized. The diesel engine is more efficient than the old steam engine. Today we are not wasting energy and we have an increasing supply. We have greater competition, falling transportation costs and much greater efficiencies of utilization. Energy is being put effectively to work to a much greater extent and much more effectively than ever before.
This leads on to another conclusion. This conclusion is that the area, or the region or the country that is able to put energy to work most effectively is the one that is likely to prosper most in economic terms. This test can be applied in the United States. For example, you find that the states of the U.S. which have the highest per capita energy consumption by and large are the ones with the highest per capita incomes. They are the most industrialized states.
In Canada, the province which puts the most amount of energy to work per capita tends to be the one with the highest per capita income. Throughout the world it almost always follows that where energy is consumed in quantity there is the greatest prosperity. This leads one to the inevitable conclusion that it is to consume which is important, and to consume efficiently, and not necessarily to produce. Canada can do both. In most forms of energy we can not only be a producer but a consumer as well. The implications for trade are obvious. We can export with more confidence as long as we export intelligently; but we should also be importing in areas where importation means lower costs than if we were self-sufficient in respect to that particular form of energy.
This applies perhaps most graphically in respect to oil. Forty per cent of the oil used in Canada is refined in the maritimes or the Montreal area. Our western Canadian crude oil does not come as far east as Montreal; it fills out British Columbia, the prairies, southern Ontario and even the Ottawa valley, but

not Montreal. It is cheaper for 40 per cent of our users in Canada to use Venezuelan or Middle Eastern oil imported into the maritimes or the Montreal area and refined there rather than bring Canadian oil all the way across Canada.
To resolve our balance of payments problem under those circumstances and to resolve it efficiently, we should basically be exporting more oil down the west coast and into the U.S. middle west; exporting it in at least as great amount as we import it from other countries into eastern Canada. This pattern will lend to the lowest cost and encourage the greatest consumption and will, I suggest, be the most rational pattern for a spread out country like Canada to follow with respect to the utilization of energy.
There are certain industries which use energy intensively. Aluminum is one example and the electro-chemical and metallurgical industries are others. We have these industries in some numbers in Canada and they are among the best equipped and most efficient in the world. They are our bread and butter industries-the resource producing industries which help pay our taxes, build roads and schools and help pay for better services generally across the nation. We should where possible encourage research in respect to the establishment of more of these energy intensive industries.
One in which I have been interested for several years is an industry which would process uranium. It is the largest single user of electricity in the United States, for example. It can upgrade uranium into a variety of forms. We do not have an industry like that in Canada but we might have one one day. For the time being we might ship our uranium to the United States, or even to the United Kingdom where a small plant exists, and have it upgraded; but as I say perhaps we will be able to do this in Canada in the 1970's or 1980's. That is the type of industry we should be sponsoring in this country.

Would the hon. member permit another question. As I understood his argument, if we had to sell our surplus energy to the United States cheaper than what the consumers of Canada have to pay for it, we should not sell it at that price. The hon. member said it must be a competitive price. In other words, if we had a surplus we must not sell it to our foreign friends at a cheaper price than the price our own consumers pay.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTION TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
In neighbouring areas of Canada and the United States-assuming Canada is the source of the energy-the price should be lower to Canadian consumers than to the consumers in a neighbouring area in the United States. Given those circumstances I would be in favour of a continuing exportation of that form of energy. The national energy board will make sure that the reserves in Canada are sufficient to look after our foreseeable requirements. This provision would also safeguard long term Canadian requirements. These would be among the stipulations which I believe can be met and are being met in respect of the export of oil, gas and power from Canada at the present time. We will have more of this trade and I suggest that this would be to our advantage and that we should not be apprehensive about it.
I want now to go on to the governmental approach-I do not mean only this government but I include all future governments as well-to energy development. It should not be unalterably opposed to export. That is one conclusion. Another is that it should be interested in focusing more of its research activity, export trade promotion, and so on, on energy intensive industries so that we make greater use of energy at home. Also I believe it should be looking across the whole spectrum of energy commodities and carefully trying to bring them on the same footing one with another. I suggest that in the long run it would be healthiest if there were no subsidies at all in respect to the various forms of energy. One form of energy subsidized more than another, for example, is not an altogether healthy situation.
We are spending more than $60 million a year at the present time on nuclear energy. That is more than $3 per person per year. I do not imagine that we will go on subsidizing the creation of a new energy industry like that forever. That is a lot of money. We are not spending anything like that on the development of oil or gas, or even on facilities for the production and transmission of electricity. We are favouring one form of energy to that extent. At the other end of the spectrum, we are subsidizing some of our uneconomic coal producing areas. These areas-should be oriented more to consumption at the pit head, and so on. We should progressively work our way out of having to move coal over vast distances, because coal does not move over great distances naturally in competition with oil and gas. Roughly $18 million a year, or $1 per person per year, is,
8902	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce being spent in this country on subsidizing an industry which could over the years readjust to a more competitive position and be in healthier circumstances.
What sort of agency do we need in government to work this out? I should have thought that a national energy board should be an energy board and should take a comprehensive approach to energy. It should not merely be concerned with interprovincial and international movements of oil and gas and the export of power, but also with developing a long term policy with respect to coal. Coal, as hon. members know, is presently administered by the coal board, which falls to a certain extent under the jurisdiction of the minister of mines. In the long term I think it would be better for coal administration to go to the national energy board and be within the orbit, as it would be today at least, of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I also think that atomic energy, this new industry which is coming along, should also be within the purview of the national energy board and that atomic energy should be taken, at least in respect to our long term programs, out of the Department of Industry and included along with the other responsibilities of the national energy board. In the United Kingdom there is a ministry of fuel and power. On the continent of Europe today there is a treaty in effect between the six nations of the European common market. They are developing a common policy with respect to all forms of energy. They are trying to put them all on the same footing eventually. The coal mining industry there is in even more serious straits, at least locally, than it is in Canada, but there are attempts to rationalize the whole energy picture and to take an over-all long term approach to the problem in individual nations and in the common market areas. I think that Canada would do well at least to organize its governmental approach to energy in a similar way.
There is only one other aspect I should like to discuss this evening and that has to do with what I might call rigidities which are creeping into the energy field. Increasingly, these forms of energy require vast investments of money for plants and equipment. A pipe line, once it is laid, cannot easily be altered or moved to another location. An oil refinery, once it is built, will continue to be located in a specific area. A large atomic energy installation, which is many more times expensive than a conventional coal or gas burning plant, is similiarly difficult to change, modify and, certainly, to move.


Consequently, you have long term contracts developing. One cannot chop and change. We do not have spot sales of products. We cannot have the same retail situation such as existed 50 or 100 years ago in respect of fuel wood, or even in respect of coal. These things involve long term investments, and do so increasingly.
We have, paralleling these long term investment situations, long term export commitments, so that contractually and financially we have an institutionalization of things. Long term planning is certainly called for, and individual firms involved in this economic activity have to plan over a long period of time. Consequently government, if it is to think in step with these industries, has to be looking a long way ahead, not just for five or ten years, but over a period of time at least as long as the lifetime of the investment, many of which run for 20, 30 or over 50 years ahead. Some pipe lines will last as long as 50 years and some power dams will last for as long as 100 years.
These investments are being made as though we know what is going to happen 10, 25 and even more years ahead, and our plans should be made in similar terms. When I say "plans", I mean our thinking, our forecasting and the whole process of decision making in this context. The thinking of private individuals and government should be in step with each other in this way.
I should like to emphasize the need for voluntary programs. I think our oil policy, a policy which has evolved over the last three or four years, has been remarkably successful. The Gordon commission studied energy, and the Borden commission studied energy even more intensively. Both commissions recommended the establishment of a national energy board. Following the establishment of a national energy board the previous government followed through effectively with other recommendations of the Borden commission. We had an oil policy which established targets in respect of exports and the movement of Canadian oil to the east and penetrating into the United States.
These targets were not set up arbitrarily by the government, but in close consultation with industry. Indeed they largely resulted from forecasts made by industry. The industry forecast that it might move oil as far east as the Ottawa valley, in respect of its eastward movement of crude oil, and remain competitive, and that it might also sell oil to the Detroit, Minneapolis and Seattle areas. These forecasts were brought into reality. The government said: These targets can be

realized; you agree that they are possible, so get on with it. The small amount of oil being imported at Sarnia, for example, dried up. Oil is no longer being imported west of Montreal. We are now exporting oil into the United States. Consequently we had a set of targets which have largely been achieved.
By 1967 perhaps we will be producing, as a result of these voluntary programs, as much as one million barrels of oil a day. That will mean this will be a billion dollar industry. The oil industry in Canada will be a billion dollar industry by 1967. That is a projection which the industry has largely made. Whether these industrial management decisions were made entirely within this country or not, it was recognized that these targets could be realized, and the government of the day decided that these things must be achieved in order to set our balance of payments right. They have come into being in order to set our financial house in order.
These things are being achieved and this is the type of voluntary program which I think can produce the lowest cost of energy consistent with an improved balance of payments and greater self-sufficiency. In other words, as some people refer to it, we have national programming. I do not think it could be properly called an indicative program because the government did not really initiate them. Rather, the industry made the forecasts and the government chose those which would yield the best over-all results.
In any event, we have experienced a program of development which not only put industry in a favourable competitive position, but lowered prices. I think this is the type of national planning that many people in this country want to see extended in respect of energy and other industries in this country. We have witnessed declining prices for energy in this country. We still pay slightly more for energy than do the people of the United States, and their price level has tended to remain about constant. I think we can move into a position of competitive advantage generally in respect to energy within the next few years.
We have always had an advantage in respect to power, mainly because public power entities do not pay income tax and have the advantage of lower interest rates. We are coming into an increasingly competitive position in respect to oil and gas, even with the United States, and this augurs well for the future. We will have more investment in energy in this development, and this favour-
Supply-Trade and Commerce able trend will be due in part to a rational program of development in which companies and associations participate, and in which the government is fully informed. This is the type of development which I believe and understand the minister favours, and I am certain it will pay dividends as years go by.

Is not one of our big difficulties in Canada in respect of the sale of oil a result of the fact that Venezuelan oil costs approximately 10 cents per barrel of crude at the wellhead, whereas it costs $1 per barrel of crude at the wellhead in Alberta? The hon. member has been referring to transportation costs. Even if you have to ship crude from Venezuela it can still be delivered in Canada cheaper than it can be produced at the wellhead in Alberta. Is that not one of the main problems?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTION TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext: I understand that Venezuelan oil, as a result of a much lower wellhead price, plus transportation costs to Montreal, is cheaper in Montreal than western Canadian crude oil. That is why, under present circumstances, it is better for us to rely on imported oil. However, one can envisage a situation where we cannot obtain our crude in this fashion because some countries are following discriminatory practices, in which case we might find it to our advantage to bring Canadian oil to the Montreal refineries. To do so would be, in my view, an act of desperation, and would only happen under extreme circumstances-that is as a result of other countries not following liberal trade policies. I think we should follow liberal trade policies.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTION TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the topic with which I intend to deal this evening may not be regarded as completely new in this chamber. I will be discussing the Northern Transportation Company and government policy with respect to crown corporations. I should like to make it clear to this committee that I am not indulging in a crusade against the activities of crown corporations, but since we are considering item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, for which the minister is responsible, I should like this evening to obtain some answers from the minister about this government's policy as it relates to the question of crown corporations, vis-a-vis private enterprise.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
On February 3 and February 4 I spoke for some time in this house placing certain facts on the record which I thought were relevant to the present competition on the Mackenzie river between Northern Transportation Company, which is a crown corporation, and the Yellowknife Transportation Company, which is a privately owned company.
I should like to begin my remarks by referring to the competition which exists between them. I think that is a good starting point. Northern Transportation, and in fact most of these crown corporations, date their start or certainly their importance from the days of C. D. Howe, who had a genius for setting up big crown corporations to get a job done quickly. I certainly have no argument with the purpose for which Northern Transportation was set up and for which the minister says they are still continuing to render service to a part of the country that needs that type of service. The question in my mind and which I should like to bring to the attention of the house is: Is it present government policy that a crown corporation should do this when private capital is ready, willing and able to do it? How far should a crown corporation be allowed to go in competing with private enterprise, when both are in the same field competing for the same business?
I have put this on record before but I should like to quote again a sentence or two from a speech by C. D. Howe in 1946. As found on page 2176 of Hansard for June 4 of that year, he said:
... it has never created a company that is in competition with private business in any way, shape or manner. If private business was able to carry out the war objective, private business was given that opportunity. The government has created crown companies only to undertake work that private industry was not willing to undertake.
That was the policy of the government at the time the crown corporation was set up. I am sure that most of the parties in the house who believe in private enterprise, and I have heard all parties except the N.D.P. campaign on that basis, feel that this is the ideal situation, that the real justification for crown companies is where private enterprise is unwilling, because of the financial risks or difficulties, or is unable because of those same difficulties to carry out a service that is essential to the country or to a part of it, perhaps to help open up a new area. But I think most of us feel that, if the original justification or excuse for setting up the crown corporation has disappeared, the day
[Mr. Nugent.)
must come when the crown should vacate and leave the field to private business.
In this regard I have asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce on several occasions for a statement on government policy at the present time in relation to private enterprise versus government enterprise. I got an answer from the minister on October 9, 1963 to a question I had asked much earlier. I suggest to the house that the answer the minister gave was far from being a clear and concise statement on the part of the government as to how far the crown corporation should go in competing. In fairness to the minister I will read two paragraphs at least of what he said. My question to the minister had been based on how far Northern Transportation was going to be allowed to go in competing in the Arctic against Arctic Shipping and on the Mackenzie against Yellowknife Transportation, and what the role of the crown corporation was. I quote from the minister's answer as found on page 3369 of Hansard:
It is the government's intention that Northern Transportation Company Limited shall continue to function as a common carrier in the Mackenzie basin and along the Arctic coast, and in so doing help to provide these areas with an efficient and dependable transportation service. In performing this function the company will, as it has done in the past, operate as a normal business corporation.
I should like to pause for a moment and repeat those words, "operate as a normal business corporation". In the past I have put on the record many instances and many ways in which this crown corporation is not operating as a normal business corporation, in that it takes unfair advantage through having avenues and advantages open to it that private corporations do not have. I will refer to this point again later. I continue the minister's explanation of the policy:
It will, for instance, continue to replace and improve its equipment when, from the viewpoint of service and economy, such action is justified, and will provide additional equipment if the volume of traffic or the development of the area indicates that such equipment is needed.
I would ask the committee to pay attention to those words regarding volume of traffic. In the last paragraph of his statement dealing with the relationship of this crown company to private enterprise the minister said:
Private enterprise is also providing service and will probably continue to do so. It seems to me that under existing circumstances both Northern Transportation and the private companies operating in the north are needed to provide a dependable and efficient transportation system.

That was the minister's statement of policy, such as it was, in 1963. I put a question on the order paper in July of 1964 to make sure I had not missed anything the minister might have said that would be more definitive as to the policy of the government, as well as to see if there had been any change. In answer to my question No. 1,588 the Minister of Trade and Commerce replied that there had been no change in government policy since his statement of October 9, 1963. If the minister has made a statement of policy in the meantime and I have missed it I apologize. However, I have been watching most closely and I do not believe I have missed anything. I do not think the question of what the government's exact policy is has been cleared up yet.
I should like to review the present position. Northern Transportation Company is a crown corporation operating as a common carrier, with tugs and barges on the Mackenzie river section of the highway to the sea. It is also a common carrier operating on the Athabasca sector in our northland and it also operates in the Arctic. On the Mackenzie section Northern Transportation Company has as competition Yellowknife Transportation Company, a private carrier, and in the Arctic it has as competition Arctic Shipping Limited, another private carrier.
It has not been the purpose of my speeches on this matter in the house to malign Northern Transportation Company or to complain of the way in which those public servants are carrying out their duties. It is a well known fact not only throughout the north but in Edmonton that Northern Transportation Company does provide a very good and reliable service to the people of the north. I have said before and I say now that I have no quarrel with the dedicated public servants working for that company who do their best, as we would hope all public servants would do, to make the company grow, to make it more efficient and to please the customers, while at the same time taking a great deal of pride in the service they render to the people of the north. That, Mr. Chairman, is exactly the course that must be followed by private enterprise companies.
My quarrel is with the policy being pursued by the government. I have pointed out in the house many ways in which the crown corporation does not compete "as a normal business corporation", to use the minister's words. The minister has said:
Private enterprise is also providing service and will probably continue to do so. It seems to me
Supply-Trade and Commerce
that under existing circumstances both Northern Transportation and the private companies.. .are needed-
Right now the government has out for tender-and I am not sure whether it has received bids and let the contract-the building of a new boat to operate in Arctic waters.
I am sure the minister must understand by now, certainly I have told him enough times, that this new boat which is to operate in Arctic waters will almost surely ring the death knell on private competition in the Arctic.
I should point out to the committee that Northern Transportation Company, this crown agency, has taken over from the Hudson's Bay Company the operations it used to undertake. It took out the Banks Land, the boat the Hudson's Bay Company had; but contrary to what was said in the house as to the purposes of that takeover, the crown corporation has not been content just to provide the service the Hudson's Bay Company was operating. In fact there has been an expansion of the service provided, and this new ship will make it possible for Northern Transportation to more than hold its own against private competition, and in fact drive out private competition from within the Arctic.
The minister owes the committee a new definition of government policy. Certainly he cannot be heard to say there is room for both when the crown corporation is deliberately pursuing a policy which is bound to have the effect, perhaps next year, of putting out of business one of its competitors in the transportation field in the north.
Next, in connection with this last statement, and I say this "last" even though it is over a year old, when the minister says, "compete as a normal business corporation" he must have his tongue in his cheek. I would like him to explain how he can call competing as a normal business corporation the effect which this will have on Yellowknife Transportation, and particularly the effect of the surplus equipment which the crown corporation has been allowed to get licensed on the Mackenzie river.
For many years it was necessary for a common carrier in that area to go to the board of transport commissioners if it wanted to put as much as one extra barge on the Mackenzie. Yellowknife Transportation had to prove that public convenience and necessity required the expansion of its fleet; in other words, that there was the volume of business that in order to handle the transportation requirements in the area an extra barge was

Supply-Trade and Commerce needed. It had to do this for every single barge, and for several years Northern Transportation had to do the same thing. I might add that Northern Transportation operating in the Athabaska sector had to do the same thing for that sector.
In the Athabaska sector Northern Transportation had no competition, and one year when there was a tremendous upsurge in the demand for transportation facilities it built a tremendous number of barges and put on some new tugs, but a couple of years later these were found more than necessary to meet the limited demands in that sector. I have requested the documents, and I could not find in the record a real application on behalf of Northern Transportation to have this system of licensing changed, so that its licences would not be for one sector or the other, but all licences issued would be automatically for both sectors.
What this meant was that Northern Transportation, a crown agency, in one fell swoop, so to speak, had all its barges in the Athabaska sector, whether surplus or not, suddenly made available to it in the Mackenzie sector in competition with Yellowknife Transportation, and was allowed to move and did move a considerable part of its fleet into that area.
It should not be necessary to remind members of the committee that a crown corporation does not have to justify its expenditures to its shareholders. It does not have the necessity of returning a dividend on its investment. Further, this particular crown corporation has the advantage of having the D.E.W. line supply and Eldorado business to give it a sufficient volume that it always has what the private company does not-a solid background of business to help to meet ordinary operating costs. I wish the minister could explain to the committee how he can pretend that this crown agency is operating as a normal business corporation when it is allowed such an advantage as that.
Next I suggest members of the committee look at some of the answers to questions I put on the order paper concerning the amount of equipment Northern Transportation has, how much it uses and the amount of freight it carries. According to the calculations I make by answers given me by the minister, Northern Transportation Company had a great many barges last year that it did not even bother to use at all. I believe it has 19 extra barges that it never had a single bit of use for during the year, and that figure does not include those it leased to Yellowknife Transportation Company.


This is the crown corporation which is now building a new boat in Vancouver. This is the crown corporation which did not itself come up with the idea of building this new boat in order to give better service. Three years previously the private company tried to bring in an L.S.M. It was a surplus vessel, but under our maritime regulations it was found too old, and could not, with due regard to our shipbuilding industry, be allowed to be brought into the country. But that did not stop Northern Transportation Company from buying it.
I believe the initial cost price was $119,000. It bought the L.S.M. and brought it into Vancouver at a time when it knew the maritime regulations did not permit the use of it. I accuse the head of the Northern Transportation Company of hoping that he would be able to get a special order in council passed so that his company would be able to move above the law and do what the private company could not do.
This boat sat there a long time, and I do not mind telling the committee that I watched very closely what Northern Transportation was doing. This crown agency, now finding it cannot use this boat, is building a new hull. It states it is going to take the propulsion machinery out of the old boat, whatever parts of it are good, and put them in the new hull at something less than what it would cost to build a completely new boat to provide the sort of service in the Arctic that the company thinks would be most efficient.
Considering the amount of money the crown agency has already tied up in surplus barges, I wonder how the minister can justify calling this method of doing business as the way a normal business corporation would operate. I am sure there is not a member of the committee who believes in private enterprise who does not doubt fundamentally whether he wants to see the government going this far, at least in policy. Do we really want to see the government go so far as to say that there is a place for competition between a crown agency and private enterprise when private enterprise is ready, willing and able to do the job? I am certain that those of us who pay lip service to private enterprise have many a doubt about that.
I know that even the members of the New Democratic party, who perhaps would have no difficulty with that first statement, are likely to object strenuously to a proposition that, in an area of the country where business undertakings are risky in the extreme and where it is a very tough and continuing task

to get private companies interested in opening up the country, these companies should have to face the fact that not only will they be in competition with a crown agency but that this crown agency will have many advantages open to it and will continue to take advantage of every natural advantage which it has. This is borne out by the situation here, where it is obvious, from the way the government let out the contract, that it is the open intention of the government that its agency should drive out private shipping from the Arctic, leaving competition only on the Mackenzie, knowing that if they are the only transport agency in the region it will make it very difficult for Yellowknife to continue transportation even on the Mackenzie; because if the destination is in the Arctic the crown agency will be the only one which can say "We can carry right through".
I mentioned some of the other tactics which have been used and how closely this situation has to be watched. Take the ordering of houses for Eskimos, for instance. They were made deliverable at Waterways, Alberta, where only the crown corporation operates, so they would be put on crown corporation barges. Why they should be delivered at that midway point is a mystery to everyone except Northern Transportation. If delivered at Edmonton they could go by road to Hay River or by rail to Waterways, and in that case both Yellowknife and Northern Transportation would have a fair chance. I say there was some persuasion on the part of the crown agency which influenced the department of northern affairs to provide for delivery at Waterways in order that Northern Transportation might not be able to compete.
Figures can be produced to show what all this has meant in terms of practical service to the people in the Mackenzie and Atha-baska sectors. The record shows that while competition between Yellowknife Transportation and Northern Transportation has existed, the unit cost of shipping has gone down. Over the last seven years shipping costs have gone down by more than 50 per cent. But in that same period, when the crown agency was the only one operating in the Athabaska sector there has been no change in the rates. I suggest this is some ground for suspecting that a little healthy competition for the crown agency is a good thing.
There is another factor which the minister should take into account when considering the policy to be followed in respect of this crown company. Where a crown company has as many natural advantages; where it has, 20220-564
Supply-Trade and Commerce as I say, the complete D.E.W. line hauling; where it has a monopoly in one sector; it is difficult for any government auditor to look at the affairs of the corporation and estimate its real efficiency. It is not so bad in the Mackenzie sector. I am not sure how close an accounting is kept, but in order to get business in that sector they have to be efficient. But what standard or guide does the government have as to business efficiency in other places? Whether you believe in private enterprise or not, if you have people in a crown corporation doing business in this way you must be concerned with their efficiency. How much is this costing the taxpayer? What gauge can be used to determine the efficiency of the operation?
I do not wish to review the whole history of the operation of these companies but I am bound to tell the committee that I think the time has come when the government should make a new statement of policy. The last clear policy statement was that made by Mr. C. D. Howe away back in 1946. The present minister must tell us what the government intends for the future. I think he would be less than honest if he did not say that of course he believes crown agencies should compete with private enterprise, even though there is private capital ready and able to do the job. Perhaps, however, he will go as far as to say it is not fair for a crown corporation to have this extra advantage. If he does, then he owes us an explanation why this crown corporation is permitted to operate in the way it does. He should inform this committee how far the exploitation of Northern Transportation is to be allowed to go. Next year, it is Arctic Shipping which will be squeezed out. How long will it be before Yellowknife Transportation will be squeezed out?
The situation is so serious now that no private shipper will want to get into the north. No one in his right mind will invest money in a transportation system which has to face competition in the manner in which the government is running this transportation system in the north. Maybe many people in this committee feel there is so little in the north that it is not worth striving for. But I think the government has said they want to expand and attract private investment. I hope the minister will have some encouraging words and be able to tell us that there is at least some hope.
