Mr. Chairman, tonight we have before us the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce and before

Supply-Trade and Commerce going into details, I should like to take a look at the expenditures for the year 1965 in order to ascertain, in terms of expenditures, the importance of that department in our present administration.
In looking at the figures at the beginning of this book and comparing the figures for the Department of Trade and Commerce with those of other departments to see where this department ranks, we find that it ranks 14th as regards the expenditures of the federal government. This is a very important department because it is somehow the general administration of trading in Canada.
But if we look at the amount of money granted or that we are called upon to put at the disposal of this department, we see that although this department is very important, in fact, there are too many departments which I think have less importance for our national economy but which on the other hand get a very large share of the budget.
When I consider the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, which is also very important, I see it comes before the Department of Trade and Commerce. There I admit that agriculture must be as important as our trade since it gets a vote of $140 million.
Now, if I consider the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I see that we are asked for a vote of $83,037,540. And if we compare those estimates with the estimates of the C.B.C., which amount to $88 million, we see that the Department of Trade and Commerce gets $5 million less than the C.B.C.
It seems to me that it does not make sense that our federal Minister of Trade and Commerce should have at his disposal only $83 million to meet the needs and obligations of such an important department. Yet, the C.B.C. has at its disposal $5 million more than the Department of Trade and Commerce. I think this does not make sense.
If you take a further look you find that the Department of External Affairs comes before the Department of Trade and Commerce. The Department of External Affairs is an important one. But, in my opinion, from the Canadian dollar point of view, it should come after the Department of Trade and Commerce.
We also have another department which I believe is far less important than that of trade and commerce; I refer to the Department of National Defence, which altogether costs the Canadian government or the Canadian taxpayers the sum of $1,525 million.

This is much more important, as far as government expenditures are concerned, than the amount which might be available to our Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I should not like to review the expenditures of all the departments but if, with respect to expenditures, we compare figures, we find that the Minister of Trade and Commerce ranks 14th. However, I think that, in Canada, trade must be placed on an equal footing with agriculture; it is a very important department.
It is silly that, in our government, some departments of lesser importance should take precedence over that of trade and commerce.
When we take a closer look at the trade and commerce estimates for which we are asked to vote $83,037,540, we note the following: general administration, $5,180,500; trade commissioner service, $6,500,000; exhibitions branch, $2,190,700; universal exhibition of 1967, $970,000; travel bureau, $4,907,300; administration of standards branch, $3,372,100; dominion bureau of statistics, $13,195,800. We notice also that there is a special vote of $46,700,000 for wheat.
This means that out of $83,000,000, an amount of $46,700,000 was allocated exclusively to wheat, or more precisely as a form of indirect assistance to the farmers of western Canada.
Now, if I add, in this same book, the number of federal civil servants directly associated-I do not say indirectly, but directly- with the Department of Trade and Commerce, I see that it employs 4,500 people.
I find it ridiculous to expect so much from our Department of Trade and Commerce and give it such a small budget.
It is a good thing to make suggestions to the department and also to voice certain criticisms; but when one realizes that the minister has so little to accomplish so many things, one cannot be surprised that his achievements should be limited.
I want to call the minister's attention to the fact that at present there is a large production of raw materials in Canada-I mean in industry-and I suggest to him that he should co-operate with his colleague the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) to try and find means to help the provinces in establishing heavy industries in Canada.
I shall give only two examples of the abundance of our raw materials. We have steel in Quebec and there is some also in the other provinces; and yet, we have practically nowhere in Canada a steel plant to process our

steel or our unfinished metal on the spot in order to turn it into a finished product.
The province of Quebec is very rich as far as steel is concerned-especially the northwestern area of the province-and it would be desirable to see a heavy steel industry settle there in order to be able to turn our unfinished production into a finished product. By the same token, we could reduce our trade deficit because, at present, our raw materials are exported to the United States to be processed and sent back to us with the consequence that the Americans take all the profits and get all the employment opportunities.
Considering that Canada has a population of over 19 million and large quantities of raw materials, it is time more than ever for the Department of Trade and Commerce to consider giving some assistance to the provinces and to co-operate with the provincial ministers of trade and industry so that we may do our own processing and keep both our raw materials and those profits we surrender to foreigners when they do the processing.
Each year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) racks his brains to find some way of reducing the balance of our international payments, the deficit balance of our national budget, and yet each year we allow almost a million dollars in profit, it was approximately $900,000,000 last year, to pass over to the United States. I do not say that all this profit was earned by the United States alone by opening up our raw materials, but this anomaly has been one of the causes of our deficit balance.
I would like to draw the attention of the minister of commerce to the fact that we are not short of anything in Canada. We have a population of 19 million. We have raw materials and crude products; yet we have men, unemployed people, engineers who would be able to establish a heavy industry for the processing of steel, asbestos and other products.
Thus we know that asbestos extracted in Asbestos and Thetford Mines is exported as raw material to the United States which is selling it back to us as a processed product. We could set up heavy industry plants in Canada, where Canadian ore could be processed and this would in turn encourage other secondary industries to produce ancillary products.
Before concluding, I should like to point out to the minister a number of anomalies in our import trade. Canada is buying from other countries machinery, implements and 20220-5644
Supply-Trade and Commerce various products that she does not have or does not produce or that we ask other people to produce. Furthermore, in the province of Quebec, we are buying heavy machinery, equipment. And the people who are selling us this machinery or equipment do not take the trouble to supply us with instruction handbooks written in French. They are glad to come over and sell us their machinery, in the province of Quebec, and to take our money; therefore, it seems to me that it would be rather easy for the Department of Trade and Commerce to call this fact to the attention of manufacturers of farm machinery, so that they may give satisfaction to our French Canadians who need these machines, but find it difficult to operate them, because their handbooks are not written in our language. There are those who do not understand English. Yet, in the province of Quebec, machinery or equipment is bought which comes from England and the United States.
In fact, the case of one of our municipalities comes to my mind. It bought some machinery from the United States and it had some difficulty to use it because there was no French handbook.
I call the attention of the minister to those facts so that he will insist that these manufacturers supply us with French handbooks which will enable us to put those machines or that equipment to good use.

EQUALIZATION OF PAY FOR PREVAILING RATES EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the system of prevailing rates for government employees known as prevailing rate employees, which exists in defence establishments and some other government branches across the country, was brought into being by order in council P.C. 3271 on December 31, 1934, a long while ago, and I suggest that it is as hopelessly out of date as would be the minimum wages that were set out in that order in council in 1934, which provided a minimum hourly wage of 30 cents for men and 20 cents for women.
Originally the government applied this so-called fair wage clause to employees who were taking part in construction and such work, and therefore it was largely tradesmen who were involved. Over the years the government has not applied to its other employees this idea of paying one level of wages in one part of the country and another level elsewhere in the country, both for the same work.
For instance, with the railways we have the same wage rate across the country; with the civil service we have the same wage rate across the country; with the military services we have the same wage rate across the country, and with Air Canada we have the same wage rate across the country; and in this era of assistance to slow growth areas I think it is obvious that the railways, civil service and military policy of paying, in slow

growth areas, the same rate as they pay in other areas has helped build up those areas. This prevailing rate policy does exactly the opposite, and has the opposite effect to minimum wage legislation.
Only the passive acceptance sometimes accorded to situations of relative antiquity has prevented earlier, massive opposition to a policy which allows Canadians to be paid different amounts of wages for doing the same work for the same government in different parts of the country. It is outdated and must go.
Over the years a number of different formulae have been applied to fix the wage rate for a trade in a particular area. Whatever is done to end this insidious system, interim pay increases should be granted meanwhile to those who are overdue for such treatment, such as the prevailing rate employees at H.M.C.S. Dockyard in Halifax. The application of prevailing rates has worked to their disadvantage. Tradesmen employed by the government in H.M.C.S. Dockyard at Halifax receive a much lower hourly rate when the formulae is applied than men working in the same trade in Vancouver, and of course as a consequence their yearly wage is considerably lower, despite the fact that residents of the Halifax area are expected to pay the same level of taxes. There is nothing but inequity in such a system and it is the very opposite of assistance for an area of slow growth.
I have been informed that the situation is being examined at present, but we want Halifax tradesmen employed by the government to receive a nationally established rate of pay, and it is not just the question of changing the formula. Anything less than a national rate of pay, the same as that provided by the railways and the military, is insufficient and inadequate.
I do not expect to receive any final answer tonight. My purpose in raising this matter is to ask that the fullest consideration be given to it. If the condition still exists when collective bargaining is brought into force for government employees-something I hope will occur in the near future-I trust this situation will be rectified at that time, because I am confident that the representations of these employees will cause that system to be done away with at an early date. We have been told that the prevailing rate employees, as well as civil servants, are to receive collective bargaining, and therefore I hope the final solution in this regard is not too distant.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I urge the government in its wisdom to see fit in the meantime to recognize how much of a contradiction this system, of prevailing rate employees receiving different wages in different parts of the country, is to its other policies. It is a situation that must end, and I hope it will end soon.

subtopic: REFERENCES TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION ON WATER LEVELS AND WATER POLLUTION

speechtext:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, Canada
Ottawa, October 7, 1964.
Mr. D. G. Chance, Secretary,
International Joint Commission,
75 Albert street,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Chance,
In order to determine whether measures within the great lakes basin can be taken in the public interest to regulate further the levels of the great lakes or any of them and their connecting waters so as to reduce the extremes of stage which have been experienced, and for the beneficial effects in these waters described hereunder the governments of Canada and the United States have agreed to refer the matter to the international joint commission for investigation and report pursuant to article IX of the boundary water treaty of 1909.
It is desired that the commission study the various factors which affect the fluctuations of these water levels and determine whether in its judgment action would be practicable and in the public interest from the points of view of both governments for the purposes of bringing about a more beneficial range of stage for, and improvement in:
(a)	domestic water supply and sanitation,
(b)	navigation,
(c)	water for power and industry,
(d)	flood control,
(e)	agriculture,
(f)	fish and wildlife,
(g)	recreation, and
(h)	other beneficial public purposes.
In the event that the commission should find that changes in existing works or that other measures would be practicable and in the public interest in light of the foregoing purposes, it should indicate how the various interests on either side of the boundary would be benefited or adversely affected thereby. The commission should estimate the cost of such changes in existing works or of such other measures and the cost of any remedial works that might be found to be necessary and make an appraisal of the value to the
two countries, jointly and separately, of such measures. For the purpose of assisting the-commission in its investigations and otherwise in the performance of its duties under this reference the two governments will upon request make available to the commission the services of engineers and other specially qualified personnel of their governmental agencies and such information and technical data as may have been acquired or as may be acquired by them during the course of the investigation.
The two governments have agreed that when the commission's report is received they will consider whether any examination of further measures which might alleviate the problem should be carried out, including extending the scope of the present reference.
The commission is requested to submit its report to the two governments as soon as may be practicable.
Yours sincerely,
Paul Martin.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, Canada
Ottawa, October 7, 1964.
Mr. D. G. Chance, Secretary,
International Joint Commission,
75 Albert street,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Chance,
I have the honour to inform you that the governments of the United States and Canada have been informed that the waters of lake Erie, lake Ontario and the international section of the St. Lawrence river are being polluted by sewage and industrial waste discharged into these waters. Having in mind the provision of article IV of the boundary waters treaty signed January 11, 1909, that boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other side, the two governments have agreed upon a joint reference of the matter to the international joint commission, pursuant to the provisions of article IX of said treaty. The commission is requested to inquire into and to

report to the two governments upon the following questions:
(1) Are the waters of lake Erie, lake Ontario, and the international section of the St. Lawrence river being polluted on either side of the boundary to an extent which is causing or is likely to cause injury to health or property on the other side of the boundary?
(2>
If the foregoing question is answered in the affirmative, to what extent, by what causes, and in what localities is such pollution taking place?
(3) If the commission should find that pollution of the character just referred to is taking place, what remedial measures would, in its judgment, be most practicable from the economic, sanitary and other points of view and what would be the probable cost thereof?
In the conduct of its investigation and otherwise in the performance of its duties under
this reference, the commission may utilize the services of engineers and other specially qualified personnel of the technical agencies of Canada and the United States and will so far as possible make use of information and technical data heretofore acquired or which may become available during the course of the investigation.
The two governments are also agreed on the desirability of extending this reference to other boundary waters of the great lakes basin at an appropriate time. The commission is requested to advise the governments when, in its opinion, such action is desirable.
The commission should submit its report and recommendations to the two governments as soon as practicable.
Yours sincerely, Paul Martin.
Friday, October 9, 1964
